32750e74423d48e7: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”

Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.

Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.
Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it.

I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.

It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?

It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.

The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.

Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.

I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.

But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?

When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.

Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.

Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial network. Now they finally realized, “If I’m going to offer mobile service, I need some form of a terrestrial network.”

At the same time, the telcos are not going to help them out. They’re not going to give them a wholesale agreement. Then when they go back and say the companies that had the lowest churn, what is the fundamental value you need in a terrestrial network? It’s low-band spectrum. Why? It travels further, you can get better coverage, and you have that connectivity.

So getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network. That’s why the stocks reacted, because people finally came to terms with the fact that Elon is actually going to build a terrestrial network.

I’m less interested in the stock and more interested in just the cost structure of how this works. If I rewind my brain to being a baby blogger at Engadget 100 years ago, the FCC told all the TV networks they had to stop broadcasting on 700 MHz and we were going to run an auction.

Verizon and AT&T bought big chunks of 700 MHz spectrum and that’s what 4G is built on. That’s the low-bandwidth spectrum that you’re talking about. It goes everywhere. This was a big victory that we reallocated 700 MHz, and 800 MHz was sitting right there the whole time. This is the Nextel spectrum. If it is so valuable, why wasn’t there a market for it until Elon showed up just now?

It was part of this transaction. T-Mobile ended up having to sell it because the government said, “If we’re going to allow you to take out the fourth competitor, which was Sprint, then in order to enable another fourth competitor out there, we need to have you guys give up some of your low-band spectrum.”

Part of the deal that T-Mobile and Sprint had with the government was that they would sell it to EchoStar. Why? Because Charlie Ergen, CEO of Dish at the time — it’s EchoStar now — was going to be the fourth competitor. This was the rationale that they gave in terms of the approval of the transaction. Dish needed low-band spectrum. The problem is Ergen went about his business, he was trying to build a network, and then he just couldn’t afford to buy that.

They had the rights to buy. Then at that point when Ergen failed on the bid to come up with the dollars to buy that spectrum, it enabled T-Mobile and actually forced them to put it up for auction. Now, your question: Why didn’t someone else show up then? Again, from SpaceX’s standpoint, as I mentioned at the start of this podcast, their strategy has been evolving over time.

In terms of the other telcos, they can’t really use it. There are some limitations that they have. But in hindsight, maybe Verizon or AT&T should have bought this 800 MHz spectrum for whatever it was, let’s call it $8 billion. They’re probably losing more in enterprise value over the concerns of what’s happening with SpaceX than what it cost them just to buy it in what’s known as foreclose. They basically just take it, even if they don’t use it or do whatever they need to meet those build out requirements and stop SpaceX from having unnecessary assets. I don’t think even these companies were taking Elon seriously and thinking that he would actually build the network.

Do you think that’s colored by the failure of Dish? We covered the promises of Dish Network to build a fourth wireless carrier in this country so closely. Their attempt was predicated on some amount of technology innovation.

They were going to build this thing called an O-RAN network, which had a more competitive supplier base instead of just Nokia or Siemens or whoever, and they were going to run it on AWS and that was going to reduce costs. Man, eventually they supported one Motorola handset in Vegas and even that was backstopped by AT&T. They literally could not do it. These promises never came true. Dish is a different company and Charlie Ergen’s a different CEO and their ability to just throw money at a problem until it’s solved is very different from Elon.

But if they couldn’t innovate to make a cheaper, faster network, what’s the evidence that Starlink can stand up an entire terrestrial network at a cost basis that allows them to compete selling service to consumers, while they’re also standing up an entire network in space? Because that feels like adding up a lot of cost.

I’m going to go back even deeper than that. Remember when Sprint was struggling, Masayoshi Son from SoftBank was claiming the same thing. They were going to cut their CapEx to nothing and they were going to use these small cells. They innovated how wireless was going to get delivered. That failed. Obviously, they had to get bailed out through the purchase when T-Mobile bought Sprint effectively for just the spectrum.

That network got completely decommissioned. To your point, Dish got a network built, but they couldn’t resonate in the market. The difference between Dish and SpaceX is Elon’s ability to get customers. That’s where Dish truly failed. They built the network. The network worked fine. They had the wholesale agreements that they needed.

I’ll push back on you a little bit there. I have a very funny email from a Dish PR person from several years ago where they said, “We’d like to issue a correction to your story. Our network does exist.” That was the level that they were competing at, where they had to insist to us that the network was real, even though we could not find it in our tests in the various cities they claim.
Maybe there was a network, they built some amount of network, but they had not built anything that competed at the national scale with the big three.

Absolutely. It’s not like your phone. The phone that I was using, I had an iPhone that it was mostly going to roam onto the AT&T and T-Mobile wholesale agreements that existed. The theory is you get the customers, you have a go-to-market strategy, and then you backfill the network. This is probably going to be something similar.

You can even go back to when John Legere first took over T-Mobile. They had a crappy network, and then Legere promised, “We’re going to build it,” taking on customers saying that the network was great before the network was great. Then it caught up because they actually finally got the Germans, Deutsche Telekom, to give them the money to invest in the network.

The same thing can happen here where SpaceX will sell something that’ll probably rely on other assets that are out there, even if the telcos themselves are circling the wagons. They have the satellites for certain benefits in terms of coverage and then they can build the capacity over time. The point is it’s going to take time. You can’t just turn on a network overnight and start selling service on that.

This has always been my framework of how to think about telecom companies. You can try to run the network cheaper or you can run some kind of different technology to make that cheaper. Or you can just spend and have the best network, which was the Verizon strategy for years and years and years.

Then you’ve got to acquire and manage your customers. That was the T-Mobile strategy. That was John Legere. He was just nicer to people than AT&T was, and he picked up a lot of customers and that drove some investment.

Then you’ve got to get some devices. You have to have the iPhone. We can set that aside because it feels like that era of competition is over. We’re not doing exclusive devices anymore. But those are the two. I’m just looking at the network here. It does not seem to me, from the outside, that Starlink is proposing to build a cheaper network.

It feels like they’re proposing to build a vastly more expensive network because they need the satellites. They’re going to launch 15,000 more satellites to support this network. Then they’re going to build a terrestrial network by investing in spectrum on the ground and building some set of base stations.

Then they’re going to have to convince one of the big three to let them roam over as some sort of mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). The big three do not want to do that. So they’re going to overcharge them for that. I’m just stuck at that being a lot of cost, even if you’re Elon Musk and you can make some set of people buy whatever you’re selling.

The third thing you said is obviously the most challenging. That’s the tent and the pole that prevents you from launching services sooner rather than later. But without necessarily getting a wholesale agreement, there might be other ways. Roaming agreements exist out there. There are roaming partners that exist that these telcos still rely on. It’s very expensive. It’s not something you can build a high-margin business on, but it perhaps provides an entry to the market sooner rather than later.

As Apple has pitched in terms of satellite connectivity, some people are in the middle of the Utah desert texting because they’re injured. There’s value there. But it’s the soccer field. We have, maybe not in the cities, but in the suburbs, plenty of areas that the telcos have effectively given up on trying to provide coverage because of NIMBY-ism, meaning people just don’t want these cell sites. This satellite coverage can give you not just this basic text messaging that Apple has been doing through the Globalstar constellation, but a true cellphone-type experience.

So that’s a positive. The second differentiation is the fact that these telcos have 60 percent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) margins. So there’s a lot of fat there that can be eaten off of, that when you’re selling other services in terms of Elon, like home broadband, maybe this becomes an entree in terms of pushing Grok and people’s usage. You don’t necessarily need 60 percent margins, in this case, for him to justify building this network.

They also talk about other data connectivity that these satellites are going to enable. Again, in the current constellation, you need a lot of power and you need a dish. But if you don’t have that, if you have the cell phone-type power, then the internet of things (IOT) and other types of opportunities that exist there become another revenue opportunity that they look at.

It’s just funny. The IOT story — that’s what all these companies promised us about 4G. That’s what they all promised us about 5G. There’s something about this business that just rhymes every time. They’re going to do self-driving cars and robot surgery. I’m confident we’re going to hear about self-driving cars and robot surgery when it comes to Starlink and Tesla and Optimus.

There’s something about these applications for next generation networks that just recurs, and we hear about them all the time. Then I think about our consumer audience at The Verge, and they want long battery life and fast service and [connectivity] all the places they go. I’m not sure how that squares with your phone is going to connect directly to a satellite in the middle of a soccer field. There’s something about that that also seems challenging.

It’s just the performance if your phone does connect to the satellite on the soccer field and it works. A lot of the things that people said wouldn’t work on Starlink in terms of airplanes or even getting customer-premises equipment (CPE) down below a certain price, they’ve delivered on. Obviously, Elon sometimes delivers on them a little later than some of his initial optimistic promises, but they ultimately get delivered on.

There is the ability with these new constellations to give you that type of connectivity on these spaces. Is that enough to differentiate with consumers? I don’t know. The telcos have attacked this by saying, “No one cares about our direct-to-device (D2D) services.” Well, your D2D services are not good. It’s just sending basic text messages. What they’re talking about is giving you that blanket coverage where you get what you expect from your cell phone wherever you go.

That’s fine, but you still have to give it to the person in the middle of the building where their cell phone works today and provide the volume at a cost that is going to be attractive to that consumer. So those are longer-term things that are going to require some amount of terrestrial network build. Then the question is: how much? A lot of the attacks that have been out there have been referencing $100 billion, $200 billion. I get that. Why?

Telcos each spend $10 billion to $15 billion a year, but they are maintaining massive customer bases. To get that initial network up where you have that usage, where you use that low-band spectrum to get into buildings, is not those types of numbers. You’re probably talking like $10 billion, $15 billion for that initial build in terms of CapEx.

The dynamic there is really interesting. I’m just thinking about AT&T when the iPhone came out. The network immediately got overloaded because there was a surge of customer demand that took four years to truly resolve. Part of that resolution was just putting the iPhone on the other carriers.

How do you think that will play out for Starlink here? Because right now, Starlink customer service is not the best in the industry. Their actual service, people love it. And then when they need customer service, it’s a bunch of automated systems and people complaining on Reddit. So there’s some challenge there if you’re running a consumer business at this scale.

For consumer businesses, think about all the advertising that’s done. The fulfillment, dealing with the phones, phone subsidies, and that’s a big part of the financing. How many customers are we talking about? So for the amount of spectrum that they have now in the network that I’m talking about for $10–$15 billion, you’re not taking 50 percent share overnight. I don’t think that would be that expectation from day one.
37102d5b045b89cc: KUALA LUMPUR: Muay Thai exponent Rifdean Masdor suffered further disappointment in Tokyo when Japanese star Yoshinari Nadaka stopped him in the second round at the Ariake Arena on Saturday.

The Sarawakian had already lost his chance to become the second Malaysian to hold a ONE Championship world title after failing Friday's hydration test despite meeting the 115-pound (52.16kg) weight limit.
The bout proceeded at a catchweight of 118.6 pounds (53.8kg), with the 23-year-old forfeiting 50 per cent of his fight purse to the ONE atomweight Muay Thai world champion.
Rifdean made his presence felt in the opening round, with Nadaka revealing afterwards that the Malaysian had broken his nose.
"For this fight, I got some damage. In the very first round, I broke my nose," said Nadaka in the post fight interview.
However, the Japanese fighter dropped Rifdean with a left hook in the first round. The Malaysian was able to bounce back to his feet to end the round.
Rifdean continued to find openings in the second round, but Nadaka delivered the decisive blow after catching a push kick.
As Rifdean attempted a spinning attack, Nadaka read the move and countered with a head kick that landed flush on the Malaysian's chin.
Rifdean went down and could not recover, prompting referee Olivier Coste to stop the contest at 2 minutes and 12 seconds.
Nadaka paid tribute to his opponent afterwards, acknowledging the difficulties Rifdean had faced before entering the ring.
He said Rifdean's conditioning might have been affected by his weight issues and thanked the Malaysian for the fight.
"Everybody, please give a big round of applause for Rifdean, too," said Nadaka.
The Japanese champion also hoped the contest had helped showcase Muay Thai to a wider audience.
"I've been doing Muay Thai since I was very young. I want to keep spreading the fun of Muay Thai to the world with ONE Championship," he said.
Nadaka's victory also earned him a 15 million yen (RM388,000) performance bonus, his first with the promotion.
"This is my first bonus. I'm very happy. It's because we had the support from all of you," he added.
Malaysian misery continued on the ONE Samurai 4 card after Hayatun Najihin "Shadowcat" Radzuan lost a unanimous decision to Japan's Itsuki Hirata in a women's Atomweight MMA bout.

3dc025af5f7ccc86: JOHOR BARU: The closure of educational institutions in Johor has been extended for another five days, from Oct 19 to 23, as haze persists and air quality remains poor.

State Education and Information Committee chairman Dr Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said the decision was made at a state haze management coordination meeting held today, in line with the wishes of Tunku Mahkota Ismail Sultan Ibrahim, Regent of Johor, who prioritises the safety, health and wellbeing of Johor residents.
"Monitoring reports show no significant change in air quality. Wind movements towards the north and weather forecasts for the next three to four days have also been taken into account.
"Health authorities have also expressed concern about the risks of prolonged exposure to air pollution, particularly among children and vulnerable groups.
A total of 30,648 cases of asthma and upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) were recorded this month, with a 20.7 per cent increase in weekly cases," he said in a statement.
Muhammad Naqib said the extended closure would depend on changes in air quality, weather forecasts and the latest health assessments.

Limited exemptions could be considered for pupils sitting certain examinations or assessments, subject to coordination by the Johor Education Department and strict health standard operating procedures, including the use of face masks and no additional activities.

He said the education department would provide daily implementation guidelines in line with Education Ministry requirements and obtain the latest feedback from the Examinations Board to coordinate examinations and assessments between schools under the ministry and Johor religious schools.
Home-based teaching and learning would continue.
Muhammad Naqib said private educational institutions and childcare centres could decide whether to operate or close, provided they operated indoors and required the use of face masks.
He said updates would be announced through the department's official channels to help schools, parents and guardians make the necessary arrangements.
Malaysia has experienced hazy conditions since early August amid forest and peat fires in Indonesia.

Muhammad Naqib said the state government understood that the prolonged closure would affect pupils' and teachers' learning routines, the management of educational institutions and parents' daily affairs.
"However, pupils' safety and health must remain the priority, while ensuring educational needs are met through appropriate approaches," he said.

"To be honest, we just wanted to enjoy the matches here at the Denmark Open. We came back from the Asian Games, had just over a week, then had to fly to Denmark," said Thinaah.
"We wanted to give our best. We did well in training, so we wanted to apply that in the tournament here."
Their passage into the final brought plenty of smiles, but Thinaah was particularly pleased with how they communicated when their game became unsettled.
"The most important thing I'm happy about is the communication we had, especially when things weren't going smoothly. We managed to pick that up quickly and turn it back around," she said.
"That was one of the crucial things we were focusing on, so that's something I'm happy about."
Pearly said facing an unfamiliar combination reinforced the importance of concentrating on their own performance and keeping their emotions in check.
"We cannot control how our opponents play, but we can control our emotions and our gameplay on court," said Pearly.
"We always try to stay alert to our own gameplay and emotions. That's important against every opponent."
Despite their satisfaction, Thinaah said there were still adjustments to make before Sunday's title decider.
"Overall, we're happy, but there are still things we need to take note of and be alert to for the next game," she added.
Pearly–Thinaah will face either Japan's Hinata Suzuki–Nao Yamakita or Sumire Nakade–Miyu Takahashi in the final.

8d18356feeda01ec: BEND, Oct 18 — Kristen Vanetsky and her family moved to Bend, Oregon, after a shooting in their New Mexico neighbourhood, choosing Silver Rail elementary for her grandson because they considered it safer.
But their world was shattered this week when a 16-year-old entered the school and opened fire, shooting dead three children and a teacher, and leaving another child and educator critically wounded.
An armed bystander who pursued the gunman into the school shot and killed him.
The tragic events, Vanetsky told AFP on Friday morning outside the school, are “unthinkable.”
The 52-year-old, whose 10-year-old grandson attends the school, said the mass shooting “just took away all the innocence” of the school’s children, disrupting their sense of safety.
She said she went to the school “trying to make sense of what’s going on.”
“Who would do this to little kids?”

Thursday’s massacre in Bend — a city of about 100,000 people in central Oregon — is the latest of 371 mass shootings that have occurred in the United States just this year, according to the tracker Gun Violence Archive.
It “just doesn’t stop,” Vanetsky said.

She said she is grateful for the actions of the man who fired back against the shooter, but notes the scenario’s inherent contradictions, which underscore the ongoing debate over gun control in the United States.
“It’s very weird, to have a gun solve the problem of a gun,” she said. “I can’t wrap my mind around it.”

“The whole thing could’ve been a lot worse had somebody not stepped in and shot the shooter,” she continued. But now, “the shooter has to live the rest of his life knowing that he shot a 16-year-old to keep other babies from being shot.”
“It doesn’t make sense,” she said tearfully.
‘Devastated’
Bend, a popular destination for its natural beauty and outdoor recreation scene, “is devastated,” Vanetsky said.
“We’re a close town of people, and we look out for each other.”
And yet, the perpetrator of Thursday’s attack was a resident of the city itself.

Authorities have not yet offered details regarding motive or any connection to the school. They did specify that a long gun was used, and media reports indicate the shooter’s mother had purchased the weapon.
“I don’t understand why a mom would buy a teenage boy a weapon like that,” said Vanetsky.
Less than 24 hours after the shooting, Silver Rail Elementary School, which serves more than 400 students, was cordoned off with yellow crime-scene tape.
A few cars and bicycles remained stranded in the parking lot.

At the school’s main entrance, neighbours and parents had created a memorial with flowers, candles and toys to honour the children — aged five, eight and 11 — and the educator whose lives were cut short Thursday.
Vanetsky said her grandson was struggling at home in the wake of the trauma he’d been through.

“My grandson should be in his classroom, with all of his friends,” she said, her gaze turning towards the school’s second floor. “Everybody should be in there learning, having fun, looking forward to their weekend, and it’s just vacant.”
“There’s nothing. Even the birds are not here.” — AFP
b32f0e3a029c0656: BANGKOK, Oct 17 — Coconut farmer Sombat Chuekrod travelled more than 200km to join hundreds on the streets of Bangkok yesterday demanding that the International Monetary Fund and World Bank change how they deal with the developing world.

Finance ministers, central bank governors and other top policymakers gathered this week in the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, as decision-makers tackle an inflation crisis fuelled by the US war on Iran and other economic shocks.

The message from the IMF has been clear: after years of economic crises starting with the pandemic and continuing through the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, worldwide debt is too high and governments need to cut spending.
For the hundreds at the protest in Bangkok, as well as for rights groups and analysts interviewed by AFP, that message is the wrong one.
“We want the IMF and World Bank to rethink their role,” said 51-year-old Sombat, as he walked alongside banners demanding reform of the institutions.
“Thai people are already poor. Please don’t make them any poorer.”
Protest organisers called on institutions like the IMF to focus on climate financing and tax reforms that aid poorer citizens rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending.

“Governments across the Global South are being forced to squeeze vital spending on public health, education, and social protection just to service illegitimate debts to wealthy nations and private creditors,” Lidy Nacpil, one of the protest organisers, said in a statement.
‘Inequality emergency’

Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the meetings, Oxfam Executive Director Amitabh Behar said the world was facing an “inequality emergency”, and that the IMF’s calls for fiscal consolidation were code for cutting spending on essential social support during the war-fuelled inflation crisis.
“It will lead to (more) price rises. It might lead to hunger,” he said. “You will see cuts further happening in terms of health, in terms of education, in terms of basic social security.
“So all that is going to suffer in a time when you actually need it more.”

The IMF this week upgraded its world economic outlook, citing unexpected “resilience” in economic growth. But it warned that that prosperity was fragmented, with vulnerable countries falling even further behind.
It highlighted oil-importing low-income countries not exposed to the boom in artificial intelligence investment as being the most vulnerable.
Yet the Fund’s advice to all countries at a time of rising global debt levels has been to cut spending and rebuild fiscal buffers after years of spending on crises.

Asked what vulnerable countries should do, IMF deputy chief of research Petya Koeva Brooks told AFP that while their situation was indeed “more difficult”, they had “no other choice” but to address their fiscal balances by either cutting spending or increasing revenues.

The IMF has proposed making energy and food subsidies offered in the wake of the Iran war more targeted, even as the UN Development Programme warned this week that if such subsidies were cut entirely, it could plunge 130 million people into poverty.
Protest organiser Nacpil questioned in an interview how one could draw a line between who deserves a subsidy and who does not.
“How poor do you have to be for them to think that you will need some support?” she asked.
Trading off
Reza Baqir of Alvarez & Marsal’s Sovereign Advisory Services said he has experience with the difficult trade-offs policymakers in low-income countries face in such crises.

“During my time as Pakistan’s central bank governor, I saw firsthand how difficult it can be for countries to balance the needs of the countries’ citizens with the needs of the IMF programme,” he said.

“At the same time, it also reinforced the importance of addressing domestic governance challenges, so countries can build their own resources and fiscal buffers, reduce their reliance on the IMF and support their citizens in a targeted and prudent manner.”

Christina Segal-Knowles of the Rockefeller Foundation said developing countries are “effectively being given two bad options” — either take on debt at currently sky-high interest rates, or make extraordinary spending cuts and potentially give up on development goals.
She proposed a “growth and investment reset” that ramps up funding to countries in need as part of a set of measures designed to provide sustained support at concessional rates.
On the streets of Bangkok yesterday, protesters prepared to spend the night under a flyover.
“We are raising our voices because we believe that the network of citizens present here are key stakeholders in the negotiations,” said activist Supaporn Malailoy.
“This is not merely a matter of borrowing money; it is about shaping the very structure and direction of the nation’s development.” — AFP
c3a2b9f0b6d12cd5: KIGALI, Oct 17 — Viewed by some as “sportswashing” and by others as an overly ambitious, grandiose project, the prospect of a Formula 1 Grand Prix in Rwanda has provoked reaction at home and abroad.
The government touts the initiative as a significant “investment in Rwanda’s future”, slated for some time in the early 2030s.
On Tuesday, Kigali put on a glitzy ceremony to announce the “historic” agreement between Rwanda, the organisation that owns Formula 1, and the International Automobile Federation (FIA).
A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organisational efficiency.
The event promises glamour — replete with champagne-quaffing celebrities — set against the backdrop of Rwanda’s verdant hills and rich wildlife, all broadcast to a global audience.
Formula 1 markets itself as the third most-watched sporting event on the planet, trailing only the Olympic Games and the Fifa World Cup.
However, the project has drawn dismay from some quarters, including Amnesty International, which immediately condemned it as an act of sportswashing.
The NGO accuses Kigali of “buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record”.
This same criticism has been levelled against Formula 1 on several previous occasions.
In its pursuit of global expansion, the sport has forged numerous partnerships with governments with questionable rights records, including China and Azerbaijan.
Sports diplomacy
Last year, Rwanda became the first African nation to successfully host the World Cycling Championships.
Through its “Visit Rwanda” campaign, Kigali also sponsors several major European football clubs, including Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), as well as the NBA’s Los Angeles Clippers.

However, while President Paul Kagame is credited with a strategic vision that has driven Rwanda’s economic transformation over his decades-long tenure, he has faced repeated accusations from opponents of suppressing political dissent.
Reacting to the news, Kenneth Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, noted on X Rwanda’s “invasion via its M23 proxy of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo”.
The armed M23 group, backed financially and militarily by Kigali, has forcibly seized vast swathes of the DRC.
During the Kigali ceremony, Kagame said it was an “honour” to be selected for Formula 1.
He described it as an “investment in Rwanda’s future” that would bring “jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come”.
But one foreign attendee voiced concerns, telling AFP in English: “I am really hoping Rwanda is not chewing what it cannot swallow.”
Formula 1 is an expensive pursuit and far wealthier nations have already seen their ambitions backfire.
The Qatar model
India and South Korea — which built circuits specifically to host Formula 1 — eventually withdrew as their financial losses mounted.
European organisers, including those in France and, more recently, the Netherlands, have encountered similar setbacks.
In comparison Rwanda, despite its economic boom, remains a low-income country with a GDP per capita barely exceeding US$1,100 (RM4,500).
It ranks 159 out of 193 countries on the United Nations’ Human Development Index, although it is steadily improving.

Critics question whether the hundreds of millions of dollars required to build a modern racetrack might be better spent on healthcare or education — not to mention the tens of millions of dollars F1 Grand Prix organisers typically charge host countries for the privilege of holding the event.
A source close to the FIA said Qatar was “supporting” the Rwandan project.
The Gulf country is also building a new international airport in Bugesera, 40km from Kigali — near where the racetrack will be constructed.
Jean-Guy Africa, CEO of the Rwanda Development Board, pointed to the “tremendous interest” from the private sector.
“You cannot miss out on the 100,000 people who will come. From a business standpoint, you stand to benefit,” he told AFP.
While several Rwandans told AFP of their pride that their country will soon host the pinnacle of motor sports, Kigali entrepreneur Amon Niyigena, took a more pragmatic view.
“The economics of hosting F1 in Rwanda will not be for everyone, but for a tiny percentage of the already rich,” he said. — AFP

cd060138da3227e2: PARIS, Oct 17 — After weeks of student protests, France faces broader, nationwide demonstrations today over the cost of living, setting up a potentially fraught six months heading into a presidential election.
President Emmanuel Macron appealed for “calm” on the eve of the protests that authorities fear could see the two movements merge, perhaps with violence.
The country’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron and his government, called today’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in an online call spread through social media.
“We’re expecting a pretty big turnout,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television.
Macron called yesterday “for calm and respect,” adding the right to protest went hand in hand with “respect for people and property”.
A police source told AFP that authorities estimated nearly 200,000 people could take part, with 40,000 in Paris.
“I have a feeling that (today) will be a sort of culmination,” 18-year-old Marie-Lou, a protesting university student in the city of Lille, told AFP.
“We’ll be joined by workers and by the Yellow Vests, who are also mobilising again. There’s a sense of hope that all these different struggles might converge.”
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered a crisis cell to monitor the demonstrations. On Thursday he said he feared clashes after what he called “urban violence” during the student protests.
Lecornu is attempting to get parliament to pass a cost-cutting budget, while protesters are demanding greater protection from inflation and more spending on public services, particularly education.
Anger at police
There is also public anger at perceived police brutality during the student protests. Several teenage protesters have been seriously injured and thousands arrested.

“It’s not just a Yellow Vest movement, it’s not just a student movement, it’s all the people who are rising up and that’s why those in power are afraid,” said Benjamin Ball, an activist working on a website for today’s demonstrations.
The unrest is weighing on the final months of Macron’s presidency, ahead of elections in April and May to choose his successor.
It has been seized upon by Opposition parties and their candidates.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in a demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, the election frontrunner according to surveys, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.
Macron this week said he believed the “legitimate” demands of the students were being “exploited for political purposes”, according to a government spokeswoman.
Prepared for violence

Organisers of today’s demonstrations have set up a website showing more than 600 demonstrations planned across France, and hundreds more protest “actions” such as blocking motorway toll booths or service stations.
Authorities and demonstrators were preparing for possible violence.

Paris police banned a major march through the tourist and business heart of the capital, and are locked in negotiations with organisers over an alternative route. The main Paris demonstration was to kick off at 2pm (1200 GMT) at the Bastille square.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure banned demonstrations around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister’s office, and the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue, among other key locations.

Nunez told France 2 that officers could use stun grenades in case of “extremely serious urban violence”. He had previously suspended their use during the student protests after one stun grenade blew off the hand of a 15-year-old.

“Disturbances are expected, especially in the demonstrations in Paris and other big cities,” an interior ministry official told AFP on condition of anonymity, citing a risk of violence from “the ultra-left movement”.
“Actions blocking major roads or large, essential facilities will not be tolerated,” the official said.
Demonstrators have set up their own smartphone app giving the real-time location of police, tear gas and helicopters. — AFP

1e54605a9dbb93b0: CAIRO: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that he would not seek to remain in office when his current term expires in 2030, describing the matter as "completely settled".

Sisi, 71, a former army general who became president in 2014, made the remarks at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, one of his flagship megaprojects.
Speaking to graduates and state officials in the sprawling new city east of Cairo, Sisi said the Egyptian constitution "would not be touched".
"The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive. This is completely settled and there will be no discussion about it," he said.
The Egyptian constitution, approved in 2014 following the 2013 military ouster of the late Islamist president Mohamed Morsi, originally limited presidents to two four-year terms.
Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and included transitional provisions allowing Sisi to run for an additional term.
Under those amendments, Sisi was re-elected in 2023 for a six-year term due to expire in 2030.
Critics and opposition figures have speculated about the possibility of further constitutional changes that could allow him to remain in office beyond 2030.
Before running for president, Sisi denied having political ambitions, but he resigned as defence minister in 2014 and entered the race, which he went on to win.

On Saturday, he said the run-up to 2030 would be used to groom a new generation of leaders, with the Military Academy training hundreds of prospective officials, ministers and presidential candidates in statecraft and leadership.

During his 12 years in power, Sisi has overseen an ambitious state-led development programme centred on megaprojects which critics say have relied heavily on borrowing and contributed to Egypt's mounting debt burden and economic pressures.
Sisi's presidency has also faced sustained criticism from international human rights organisations over restrictions on political opposition, civil society and freedom of expression.
The government rejects these allegations, saying its policies are necessary to preserve stability and security.
34868059a4ad7fa5: PARIS: Protesters clashed with police in Paris and other cities in France on Saturday during nationwide rallies over high prices as the country heads towards a presidential election.

The country's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
It appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in the protests on the first day of half-term holidays.

"We're here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality," said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.
An AFP photographer also saw some protesters attack a police building in the city.
'We're suffocating'

"At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren't," said Franck, a civil servant in his forties who would not give his surname, as he demonstrated in the central town of Gueret with around 300 people, a quarter of them high school students.
"We can't take it anymore, we're suffocating," he added.
In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.

Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.
"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he told AFP.
In Paris, where the authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website set up by organisers on the eve of the protests.
Fuel price hike
Around 45% of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
Purchasing power in France has dwindled since 2024, while the price of fuel has soared since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year.
The eurozone's second largest economy is struggling to reign in its public debt, projected next year to reach more than 120% of GDP – double the EU limit of 60%.
Economists say significant debt reduction will come only with major reforms, such as sharply curtailing France's generous pension system.
Macron on Friday evening called "for calm and respect", adding the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property".
France's far-left and far-right parties have both seized upon the unrest.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.
fb1bb664b2782767: KUALA LUMPUR: Alien species of fish comprise as much as 95% of the fish population of Ampang Hilir lake, posing a serious threat to the balance of the country's freshwater ecosystem, a senior agriculture official said.

Isham Ishak, secretary-general of the agriculture and food security ministry, said the ministry is reviewing efforts to tighten existing regulations, including the possibility of banning certain fish species identified as threatening the local ecosystem.

He called for greater efforts to curb the problem of foreign fish species being introduced into public waters, including community education to stop the practice of releasing unwanted pet fish into lakes, dams, and public irrigation areas.

"If we do not educate the public, this matter will become a culture that is difficult to curb and will become a long-term problem," he said as the introduced fish could harm aquatic biodiversity and threaten the survival of local fish species.
Data from the fisheries department show that of the 154 fish species recorded in Ampang Hilir lake, 146 were foreign and eight were local.
Isham was speaking at an event to hunt foreign fish species at the lake. The event, which has been carried out since 2022, resulted in a total catch of 19.7 tonnes of alien species.

He said among the measures needed were to increase the catch of foreign fish, to release more local fish fry to help balance the population, and to prevent the public from releasing pet fish into public waters.
He also said that the ministry is reviewing efforts to tighten existing regulations, including the possibility of banning certain fish species identified as threatening the local ecosystem.
At today's event, Agrobank released 1,400 local fish fry into the lake, consisting of 1,100 baung fish and 300 lampam sungai fish, to help support the conservation of local species.

Meanwhile, Agrobank chief development officer Ahmad Arif Abu Bakar said that efforts to restore the balance between local and foreign fish populations need to be supported by increasing public awareness and education on the importance of preserving the country's biodiversity.
"The public needs to understand their responsibility in maintaining the ecosystem, including not releasing pet fish into rivers or lakes when the fish grow larger," he said.
About 250 people took part in today's event to catch alien fish using seine nets, cast nets, fishing lines and fish traps.
c40816a027943218: VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV will leave the Rome hospital where he has been recovering from lung cancer surgery on Saturday after doctors deemed him "fit for discharge", the Vatican said.
Leo, 71, has been at Gemelli Hospital in Rome since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung to extract a cancerous tumour.

"Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge," doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora wrote in a note published by the Vatican.
The Vatican said Pope Leo "will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow he will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment".
The Angelus prayer is typically delivered by the pope from the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter's Square.
But in previous years, former popes John Paul II and Francis, who were also hospitalised at Gemelli, delivered the prayer from the windows of their hospital rooms.
The Vatican press office said Leo celebrated mass on Saturday, as he has in recent days, in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where he has been recovering.
Outside the hospital, 12-year-old Ukrainian Varvara Struck told AFP she was rooting for the pope.
The former cancer patient said she had met the pope last year in Rome, "and he blessed me for a successful treatment".
"With his support, I've now overcome my illness, and I want to give him my positive energy so that he, too, can overcome his illness as quickly as possible," she said.
News that the otherwise active pope had a cancerous tumour removed from his lung has rattled the Vatican and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
But his doctors have said Leo's recovery has been progressing normally as they await the results of tests that will determine the course of action to take.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Up in the air, however, is a planned papal trip to South America, scheduled for November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Vatican watchers say Leo — who spent two decades as a missionary in Peru — is anxious to make the long journey but will likely follow his doctors' recommendations.
Leo has cancelled all his audiences until Oct 20.
The pope announced to the public in St Peter's Square last Sunday, following the Angelus prayer, that a routine medical examination had revealed a nodule that doctors recommended should be removed.

dd874e888efafa9b: NEW DELHI, Oct 17 — India’s Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention today, a day after his arrest during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority.
Dipke, 31, was detained yesterday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital’s central Connaught Place district.
He walked out of a police station this afternoon, waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away, an AFP photographer saw.
“Abhijeet Dipke released,” CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 after entering Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

Rights groups and critics however say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects. — AFP
1f8ed0c371d88e94: PETALING JAYA: Backbencher Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) akan memastikan kerajaan Sarawak terus dipantau sekiranya GPS berjaya menyapu bersih semua kerusi pada PRN akan datang, kata Menteri negeri Abdul Karim Rahman Hamzah.
Karim berkata 'backbencher' akan bertindak sebagai kumpulan pendesak seperti pembangkang sekiranya GPS memenangi semua 82 kerusi dalam pilihan raya itu, lapor Dayak Daily.
“Kita mempunyai mekanisme semak dan imbang sendiri, termasuk unit ombudsman dan mekanisme lain untuk memastikan akauntabiliti,” katanya yang dipetik sebagai berkata.
GPS kini memegang 80 daripada 82 kerusi dalam DUN Sarawak, manakala baki dua kerusi, Padungan dan Pending, diwakili DAP.

Karim yang juga ketua penerangan Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), parti utama GPS, memberitahu FMT tahun lalu bahawa kerajaan negeri pimpinan GPS mempunyai mekanisme semak dan imbang yang mencukupi meskipun terdapat kebimbangan mengenai ketiadaan pembangkang yang kuat.
Pada November 2023, Sarawak menjadi negeri pertama yang menubuhkan unit ombudsman melalui undang-undang selepas Rang Undang-Undang Ombudsman Sarawak diluluskan di DUN.
Bagaimanapun, pada 2025, Pengerusi DAP Sarawak, Chong Chieng Jen menuduh kerajaan negeri sengaja melengah-lengahkan pembentangan laporan daripada unit itu.
fe92bea3f879c7ee: JAKARTA: Indonesia has deployed a total of 2.4 tonnes of dry ice over South Sumatra in a two-day weather modification operation aimed at dispersing thick haze caused by forest and land fires.

National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) Disaster Data, Information and Communication Centre acting head Berton Panjaitan said the operation, conducted from Oct 15 to 16, initially focused on the area around Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport in Palembang, where thick haze had disrupted flights.
"The weather modification operation over the two days involved three flights, with a total flying time of seven hours and three minutes," he said in a statement on Saturday.
South Sumatra is among six provinces prioritised by Indonesia for forest and land fire prevention and response, alongside Riau, Jambi, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan.
A total of 189 high-confidence hotspots had been recorded in the province as of Friday night.

Berton said dry ice was being tested as an alternative method to disperse haze by weakening atmospheric conditions that trap smoke near the ground, potentially allowing it to rise and improve visibility.
He said visibility at the airport improved from 1,000 metres to as much as 3,000 metres during the operation, creating more favourable conditions for flight operations.
However, he acknowledged that further research was needed to determine whether the improvement resulted from the dry ice treatment or other weather factors.

Separately, the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) said in a statement that smoke from forest and land fires briefly reached the atmosphere over Greater Jakarta on Friday but had begun moving away on Saturday, with no evidence of an impact on ground-level air quality.

According to the agency, air quality across Jakarta ranged from good to unhealthy on Saturday, with levels of fine airborne particles (PM2.5) in Kemayoran, Central Jakarta, recorded at between 46.7 and 109.7 microgrammes per cubic metre.
3f7e90810183cd15: BANGKOK, Oct 17 — International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva said today this year’s Annual Meetings with global policymakers were marked by “optimism and worry” about the global economic outlook as the event wound down in Bangkok.
Georgieva also said her organisation had a “responsibility” to help low-income countries struggling with price shocks stemming from the US-Israel war on Iran.

Meetings in the Thai capital this week brought together finance ministers, central bank chiefs and other top officials from around the world, with surging inflation, spiking bond yields and economic growth driven by artificial intelligence at the top of the agenda.
“(The meetings) were marked by both optimism and worry,” said Georgieva, who was speaking at a press briefing alongside Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan.

“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia. But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry, and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”

All week, the IMF has warned that high levels of debt and rising bond yields in advanced economies are tightening financial conditions just as central banks need to focus on bringing inflation down, likely by increasing interest rates.

Global energy prices have spiked since late February, when the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran, with Tehran’s retaliatory actions targeting Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailing oil and gas supplies.
The price increases have rippled across the globe, fuelling inflation in economies across a range of income groups.
The most vulnerable to the shock, the IMF has said, are low-income oil-importing countries that are not exposed to the boom in AI investment that has propped up growth in many advanced economies.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, they don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” said Georgieva.

She said such countries needed to set spending targets such that they prioritised growth and protecting the most vulnerable people, adding that the Fund had a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
Higher global interest rates and bond yields, however, were driving up debt repayments for low-income countries, she said.
The share of debt repayments as a percentage of government revenue had gone up from 8 to 14 per cent for low-income countries in recent years, the IMF chief said.

She said her organisation had a responsibility to help countries to restructure debt if needed; to assist with domestic resource mobilisation; to bring in international finance; and to create conditions for private investment.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people.”

On the AI investment boom, Georgieva said that member countries had recognised its value in propping up growth, but “when we are dependent on one particular driver of growth, it is like we stand on one leg”.
A key debate at this year’s meetings has been on whether the technology’s most advanced frontier models require regulation and guardrails.
The question has grown more urgent after recent revelations of security incidents involving autonomous AI agents.
Georgieva said she was “impressed” by the spirit of cooperation between AI companies, governments and other stakeholders that she witnessed in Bangkok on the issue. — AFP
fa09dd359bda4425: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, according to three people familiar with internal discussions.
Trump is not on the Nov 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilise voters who might otherwise skip the election.

He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.
Much of the friction has centred on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism.
Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation.

As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.
"What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said.
Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.
Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration.
Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterisation, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation". Wiles did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has long distanced himself from political setbacks

Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost.
More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections.
But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances.
His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war.

Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, travelled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia.
The New York Times reported that the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections.

Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an Oct 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!"
Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said.
One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers.
For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said.

In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same."
In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms.

That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year. Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a fight is not worth responding to."
US$200 million and redistricting

With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at US$200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said.
Trump has also pressed political aides and advisers in the past week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver clearer Republican gains, two sources said.
Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state's congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did in the 2024 election.
Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. S
ome Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage.
"The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said.

Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a "short leave of absence". But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one of them said.

It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term.
Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

ab2594c9143faa43: KOTA BARU: More than 65,000 foreigners were detained for various immigration offences in over 11,000 enforcement operations nationwide from Jan 1 to Oct 15, said Immigration Department deputy director-general (Operations) Datuk Lokman Effendi Ramli.
He said more than 146,000 foreigners were checked during the 287-day period, while over 45,000 of those detained were repatriated to their respective countries.
The department conducted an average of more than 38 operations a day, checking about 511 foreigners and detaining 228 daily, he said.

"This shows the seriousness of the Immigration Department in continuously enforcing measures to combat immigration law violations in this country," he said at a press conference after an enforcement operation at the Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) Specialist Hospital construction site in Kubang Kerian here today.

Lokman said the most common offences included failing to possess valid documents or permits to stay in Malaysia under Section 6(1)(c) of the Immigration Act 1959/63, overstaying under Section 15(1)(c) of the same Act, and abusing passes or permits.
He said visa abuse included entering the country on a social visit pass but working without valid permission.
Nationals of Bangladesh, Indonesia and Myanmar were among those most frequently repatriated following enforcement operations, he added.
The operations covered various sectors, including construction, services and agriculture.
In a related development, the department detained 55 foreigners out of 57 people inspected during a raid at a construction site in Kubang Kerian today.
Lokman said they were detained on suspicion of various immigration offences and brought in for further checks before legal action was taken.
In a separate operation at 8.30am today, the department detained a Myanmar man suspected of acting as a transporter to smuggle 10 of his compatriots out of Malaysia through illegal routes.
All 11 individuals, aged between 20 and 34, were arrested at a hotel in Wakaf Che Yeh here.
Lokman said the 10 Myanmar nationals were believed to have travelled from Johor Baru and Kuala Lumpur before transiting in Wakaf Che Yeh to be smuggled out of the country.

"Each individual is believed to have been charged around RM3,500 to be smuggled out of the country. However, as a result of intelligence, their movements were successfully intercepted and all of them were detained for further investigation," he said.
He said investigations were ongoing to establish how long the suspected transporter had been involved in the activity and whether other groups were involved.
Lokman said smuggling foreigners through illegal routes was not a new issue and could involve several groups or agents, but investigations into the case were continuing.

7babd23a0cb78db9: RAWALPINDI: England, Sri Lanka and hosts Pakistan meet in a one-day international tri-series starting in Rawalpindi from Sunday as they build up to next year's 50-over World Cup.
With the global tournament – co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia – a little under a year away, Pakistan captain Shaheen Shah Afridi described the series as vital.
"It will be important we do well as the focus will be on the World Cup and we need to get good preparations," Shaheen said ahead of his team's opener, against Sri Lanka on Sunday.
While all three sides are former World Cup champions, their recent results are less encouraging.
Pakistan, champions in 1992, have not qualified for the ODI World Cup semi-finals since 2011 and finished fifth at the last World Cup in India three years ago.
England won the title at home in 2019 but fared miserably in 2023, coming seventh.
The 1996 champions Sri Lanka were no better.
Pakistan will see the return of ace batsman Babar Azam after he was not selected for the Twenty20 series against Sri Lanka which finished last week with Pakistan winning 2-1.

England skipper Harry Brook said: "It's a great opportunity against two very strong sides and will hold us in good stead, and if we play the final it will show us where we stand," said Brook, whose team meet Pakistan on Tuesday.
All teams play each other twice before the top two clash in the Oct 31 final in Lahore.
England are without star batter Jos Buttler (injured) and fast bowler Jofra Archer (rested).
But they are on the back of three successive ODI series wins – two against Sri Lanka and one over India.
Sri Lankan skipper Kusal Mendis was in positive mood.
"We have plans in place (towards the World Cup) and I hope the team shows some good progress," said Mendis.

b717a09d90c89173: BANGKOK: The artificial intelligence boom has been a key driver of global growth but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday.
The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3% between 2023 and 2025 – a figure she said would be closer to 4.6% without AI-related products.
"It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday.
"You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning."
But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment.
Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy".

"The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world".
"If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said.
An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4% by 2028.
"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said.
War and regulation
While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on, it could "puncture" the boom.

They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models".
"A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said.
The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook.
Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks.
Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment.
"If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok.
86ed94b0d743ba85: KLUANG, Oct 17 — The Malaysian Civil Defence Force (APM) is strengthening its preparedness for the Northeast Monsoon (MTL) by operating its operations control centres around the clock to coordinate emergency responses and disaster relief.

APM Deputy Chief Commissioner (Operations) Ghazali Abd Rahman said the move was backed by improved communication systems and closer coordination with agencies on disaster management committees at various levels to address the risks of floods, water surges and landslides.
He said communication between the southern, eastern and central zones would be improved to ensure effective coordination and allow personnel from other zones to be deployed to disaster-hit areas.
“Effective communication between zones will enable additional members to be deployed to support the more than 12,000 personnel on standby for the 2026/2027 MTL.
“We will mobilise support teams from the respective zones and work together across zones to conduct exercises and assist one another during disasters,” he said.
He was speaking after the closing ceremony of the 2026 APM Strategic Partnership Programme with the Media for the Southern Zone at the Southern Region Civil Defence Training Centre here today.
Ghazali said APM was also stepping up preparedness by improving personnel skills, maintaining and expanding its assets and logistics to ensure smooth rescue operations throughout the monsoon season.

He also welcomed the increase in allowances for APM volunteers announced in Budget 2027 by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, with rates for personnel rising from RM8 to RM9 and those for officers from RM9.80 to RM10.80.
“Although the increase may seem small, it will boost morale and encourage personnel to provide the best possible service to the public and the country,” he said. — Bernama
*Editor’s note: The abbreviation APM in Malay stands for Angkatan Pertahanan Awam Malaysia, or the Malaysian Civil Defence Force. MTL stands for Monsun Timur Laut, or the Northeast Monsoon.
f3e2e132c6cc0074: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 17 — National women’s doubles pair Pearly Tan and M. Thinaah ended Malaysia’s 18-year wait for a place in the Denmark Open final after defeating China’s Bao Li Jing-Cao Zi Han in today’s semi-finals.

e8fb198955c83076: PETALING JAYA: Backbenchers from Gabungan Parti Sarawak will keep the Sarawak state government in check if GPS manages a clean sweep at the next state election, says state minister Abdul Karim Rahman Hamzah.

9e559b8bf19c8197: JAKARTA, Oct 17 — Indonesia has deployed a total of 2.4 tonnes of dry ice over South Sumatra in a two-day weather modification operation aimed at dispersing thick haze caused by forest and land fires.

National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) Disaster Data, Information and Communication Centre acting head Berton Panjaitan said the operation on Oct 15 to 16 initially focused on the area around Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport in Palembang, where thick haze had disrupted flights.
“The weather modification operation over the two days involved three flights, with a total flying time of seven hours and three minutes,” he said in a statement on Saturday.

South Sumatra is among six provinces prioritised by Indonesia for forest and land fire prevention and response, alongside Riau, Jambi, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan, with 189 high-confidence hotspots recorded in the province as of Friday night.

Berton said dry ice was being tested as an alternative method to disperse haze by weakening atmospheric conditions that trap smoke near the ground, potentially allowing it to rise and improve visibility.
He said visibility at the airport improved from 1,000 metres to as much as 3,000 metres during the operation, creating more favourable conditions for flight operations.
However, he acknowledged that further research was needed to determine whether the improvement resulted from the dry ice treatment or other weather factors.

Separately, the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) in a statement said smoke from forest and land fires briefly reached the atmosphere over Greater Jakarta on Friday but had begun moving away on Saturday, with no evidence of an impact on ground-level air quality.

According to the agency, air quality across Jakarta ranged from good to unhealthy on Saturday, with levels of fine airborne particles (PM2.5) in Kemayoran, Central Jakarta, recorded at between 46.7 and 109.7 microgrammes per cubic metre. — Bernama
