70c732a9a0197878: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.

Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?

Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33.

But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again.

Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment.

Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded.

The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019.

Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes.

Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times: “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.”

Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal.

A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant.

Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032.

It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that.

Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors.

cfb3c2ddc081661a: Have you ever thought about what makes you you? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.
EDDIE GUY
Head transplant

White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.

The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.

Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One, all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily.

Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.”
“There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email.
Mindclones

Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities.

While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.”

Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality.

What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered, “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar.
Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.
Brain in a jar

So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood.

The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ.

Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.

What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks.
EDDIE GUY
Gradual brain replacement

On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging, that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones.
We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue.

Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied.

Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body.

We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too.
Brain upload

Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says.

Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere.

Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A survey of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in PLOS One, estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125.

That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated.

But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer.
EDDIE GUY
Synthetic neocortex
That’s right: an extra brain.

Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language.

The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.”

Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine.

Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-­funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-­engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts.

The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.”

Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”
bb8da7cf13f68595: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.

The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed.
The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field.

“Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.”

“Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.”
Buying time

Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years. But there’s plenty of room for improvement.

One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs.

People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer.

The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand.
“With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger.

Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder.

Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through.

Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.

When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.

The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023. Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats.

Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100.

It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.”
Deep-freezing kidneys

The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab.

There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours.

The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it.

It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof.

Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack.

After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year.
Pink right up

The real test of these kidneys comes when they’re taken out of the freezer, rewarmed, and flushed of their chemicals and nanoparticles. Can they support life? So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways.

In one set of experiments, the researchers put rewarmed kidneys on perfusion devices—systems that are already used in transplant surgeries both to provide organs with nutrients and to help doctors assess them while they’re out of the body.

In another set of experiments, Finger and his colleagues transplanted rewarmed kidneys into pigs and monitored them for two hours. In both experiments, the rewarmed kidneys seemed to recover, says Finger. “They pink right up,” he says.
COURTESY OF THE RESEARCHERS

There are lots of ways to measure the function of a kidney, but one key test is whether or not the organ can make urine. By this measure, the rewarmed kidneys did well, although they produced around two-thirds of the amount that would normally be expected. “They produce urine … within a minute or so,” says Finger. “We know that they work.”

Most of the rewarmed kidneys had been banked for days or weeks. But one had been in the freezer for just over a year. When Finger and his colleagues rewarmed it and put it on a perfusion machine, they found that it produced urine “immediately.” “It actually looked better than many of the [other] kidneys,” says Finger. “We’re comfortable now saying we can store them for a year and rewarm them with excellent function.”

“It’s a very big deal to go a year,” says Kevin Myer, president and CEO of LifeGift, an organ procurement organization based in Texas. Being able to store organs for that length of time would transform organ transplantation. He envisions banks of organs that could be used on demand in emergency cases where people can’t wait, such as for some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds.
Final hurdles

But the procedure isn’t ready for prime time just yet. As well as producing less urine than expected, the rewarmed kidneys also showed signs of injury. The damage seems to be caused by the cryoprotectant chemicals, say the researchers.
“This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem,” as Kilbride puts it.

The team has shown that the rewarmed kidneys can regain blood flow, which is “very important,” says Greg Fahy, a cryobiologist who is considered a pioneer in the field. But he’s worried about the extent of the damage to the organs. “We can’t tell from these experiments whether these kidneys might have supported life or not.”

But Fahy, who is chief scientific officer at the biotech companies Intervene Immune and 21st Century Medicine (where he is also executive director), acknowledges that it’s not clear how these kidneys might fare once they’re inside a living animal for the long term.

Finger also hopes to find ways to repair the damage seen in the kidneys. Other research has shown that the health of transplant organs can improve while they’re on perfusion machines. And damaged kidneys might undergo some level of self-repair once they’re in a body. At any rate, human kidneys may cope better with the process than pig kidneys, says Finger.

The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs over longer periods of time. The team, along with many other researchers in the field, will continue the search for less toxic cryoprotectants, too. Finger, Bischof, and their colleagues are also planning experiments with human kidneys.

Finger is optimistic. “We’re going to see that there’s injury, and it’s not perfect … but now we’ve got to the point where it works,” he says. “These are big, historic milestones in our field, and we’re excited about it.”
548342f77b75d402: From Lim Teck Ghee
In Selangor, a voter in Sabak Bernam has roughly six times as much say in who goes to Parliament as a voter in Bangi. Nationally, the largest seat has about 10 times the voters of the smallest.
That is not "one person, one vote".

This can be fixed before the next general election (GE16) without amending the Federal Constitution and without any state losing a single seat. The window is open now. The eight-year constitutional freeze on redrawing peninsula boundaries ended in March 2026, and the Sabah and Sarawak freezes have also lapsed.
But the clock is short: every step must be completed before Parliament is dissolved for GE16. If it is not, the next election will be fought on the 2018 map.
At a glance

The problem: some voters' ballots carry six times as much weight as others', even within the same state. The fix: redraw boundaries so no seat is more than one-third above or below its state's average.

What it needs: a simple majority in the Dewan Rakyat. No constitutional amendment. No state loses a seat. The deadline: the report must be passed before Parliament dissolves, no later than Dec 19, 2027.
There are more than 300,000 voters in Bangi, Selangor. There are about 51,000 voters in Sabak Bernam in the same state. There is a 6:1 value difference between their vote power.

Population growth, urban migration and the Undi18 reforms – automatic voter registration and lowering the voting age to 18 – added millions of new voters, many in fast-growing urban and suburban seats such as Bangi and Damansara.
The 2018 boundaries were not drawn for this electorate. The result is a map in which where you live decides how much your vote is worth.
Why it matters to every Malaysian
Equal voice: every citizen's ballot should carry roughly the same weight. Today, it depends on your postcode.
Fair competition: lopsided boundaries let parties win majorities that do not reflect how people voted and have long-fed suspicion of gerrymandering.
Better service and fairer spending: one MP cannot properly serve 300,000 constituents. Over-represented areas also attract a disproportionate share of political attention and public money.
Trust in elections: a transparent, data-driven review rebuilds confidence in the Election Commission (EC) and gives young and first-time voters a reason to turn out.
The plan: the one-third rule, applied within each state

Section 2(c) of the 13th Schedule of the Federal Constitution already says the number of electors in each constituency within a state ought to be approximately equal while allowing some extra weight for hard-to-reach rural areas.
The plan simply gives that principle a measurable target.

No state gains or loses seats. Perlis keeps three, Pahang keeps 14, Selangor keeps 22. Calculate each state's average number of voters per seat. Redraw the boundaries so every seat falls within one-third (±33%) of that average, aiming for ±25% wherever geography allows. Rural weightage stays, but within a defined limit.
For example, Selangor's 22 parliamentary seats have an average of about 167,000 voters each. Under the one-third rule, each seat would have to have between 111,000 and 222,000 voters.
Shrinking Bangi and enlarging Sabak Bernam – and doing the same across the state – brings every Selangor seat into a defensible range.
Why this is legal and politically passable
Redrawing boundaries inside each state needs only a simple majority to approve the EC's report in the Dewan Rakyat. The 2018 report passed this way.
Changing how many seats each state has would mean amending Article 46, which needs a two-thirds majority (148 of 222 MPs). This plan leaves Article 46 untouched.
The timing is lawful. Article 113 allows a review once eight years have passed since the last one and requires it to finish within two years. The peninsula freeze ended in March 2026.

It has been done this quickly before. The previous peninsula review, begun in 2016, went from start to Dewan Rakyat approval in roughly 18 months. The maths works, the constitution allows it and the timeline is viable. What is missing is the decision to start.
Sabah and Sarawak: complementary, not competing

The federal government has agreed in principle to restore Sabah and Sarawak to one-third of Dewan Rakyat seats, in line with the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63), and talks with the EC have begun. That is a separate track, as adding seats requires amending Article 46 by a two-thirds majority, plus wide consultation.
The two reforms should run in parallel. Fixing the gaps within each state does not depend on the outcome of the MA63 seat talks – and must not be delayed while those talks continue.
The clock
From now until December, the EC must formally notify the speaker and prime minister. The first proposed maps would then be gazetted and displayed publicly for a month.

From January to March 2027, the first round of local enquiries would hear objections. From April to June 2027, the EC revises maps where justified and puts them up on display for a month if revisions are made.
From July to September 2027, the second round of local enquiries would be held, after which the EC would submit its final report to the prime minister.

From October to November 2027, the report would be tabled at the budget sitting and passed by a simple majority. The royal order could then be made and gazetted before Parliament is dissolved automatically on Dec 19, 2027, if not earlier.
This is tight but achievable, provided the EC begins before the end of 2026 and Parliament is not dissolved before the report is passed.
Answering the critics
“Isn't this too rushed?” The constitution allows two years; this plan uses about 18 months, matching the last peninsula review.
“Who benefits politically?” Voters do and the nation too. Some safe seats will become competitive, which is why incumbents of every party may object.
Call to action
The EC must formally commence the review before the end of 2026.
The prime minister must commit to tabling the final report promptly and to not dissolving Parliament before it is decided.
All MPs and political parties must pledge publicly to support a fair, within-state realignment, regardless of its effect on their own seat.
A fairer map before GE16 is within reach. All it takes is the political will to begin.
(Voter figures are based on the GE15 electoral roll).
Lim Teck Ghee is a public policy analyst.

bdb5f9d6d0998937: As artificial intelligence use becomes more widespread, scholars are working to understand its effects on the people who use it. MIT Professor Eric So offers one of the most complete syntheses yet, in his new book, “The Collision: What AI Does to Us,” published this month by W.W. Norton. Recognizing that AI offers opportunities to complete work faster, and in some cases has been turned into useful domain-specific tools, So nonetheless looks at the costs of relying on it too broadly. He contends that heavy use of AI can lead to a kind of cognitive atrophy, in which people fail to develop and retain essential thinking skills. In general, he says, evidence shows that our ability to learn gets dramatically better when we wrestle with material, work through initial failures, keep iterating, and in the process acquire better thinking skills while retaining more knowledge.  These conclusions are drawn from recent research by So and others, in academia and industry, including analysis from AI firms themselves, such as an Anthropic study showing that about half of queries from college students were low-effort queries for simple answers. So also weaves personal reflections into his narrative — having long studied financial markets and behavior, he is familiar with analyzing how new tools and information affect our decisions. MIT News talked to So, who is the Sloan Distinguished Professor of Global Economics and Behavioral Science in the MIT Sloan School of Management, about the book.  Q: What prompted you to write “The Collision”?    A: I wrote this book in response to patterns I was seeing in myself and other individuals. I open the book with this story where I was instinctively reaching for AI to help me think through problems I normally would have handled myself. A colleague had reached out for assistance and I had essentially taken her question and written half a sentence, then said, “ChatGPT, help me finish this professionally.” I made a few light edits and sent it off. And I sat back and really felt incredibly concerned about how I had removed my own thinking from the process. I have found students are outsourcing their thinking to AI, rather than thinking through things themselves, turning to it to answer homework that would normally help them build mastery in a subject. We need to start understanding what this technology is doing to us and how it interacts with human cognition and our psychology, and give people some practical insights.  Q: Part of that means understanding the incentives people have to use AI, or how the allure of AI takes hold, even when there are long-term costs, in your view.  A: There are converging factors drawing us to AI. For example we have a real biological instinct to conserve our mental energy, and socially, we face situations where AI is used by other people to race ahead, and it rachets up the pressure on everyone else to use AI. Combine that with the problems detecting AI use in a practical way, and all these factors create what I call “AI gravity,” this constant pull to use AI. It’s not simply a matter of telling people to think for themselves. At this moment we’re in, AI is colliding with society. Q: So we need to look at these systemic factors, not just individual decisions, when it comes to AI use, like businesses urging employees to use it.  A: Many organizations are not just suggesting use of AI: It is now the basis of your evaluation, meaning if you want a bonus or promotion, it is incumbent upon you to use these tools. I think a subtle process is taking hold in academia, where people say, “My future employer will want me to use AI, so I’d better start using it now.” But the problem is that as you start to use AI now, we’re losing touch with the practices and capabilities we’re seeking to build, and in turn that makes us more dependent on using AI in the future, and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Q: What is AI doing to our minds?  A: AI is not just changing what we can do, it’s changing who we are as thinkers. AI removes a lot of the friction necessary to build foundational mastery. It is causing many people to lose their capacity for pushing through problems. AI offers instant relief, and we become accustomed to that. Many people are turning to it as an access point for information, so it’s affecting our ability to remember. Also, AI is changing our interpersonal relationships. A key point in the book is that these models are simultaneously sycophantic, meaning they want to make us happy because that’s how they drive engagement and get positive feedback, but they are also really persuasive. We lose the ability to connect with other people because we’re so accustomed to this frictionless environment where the models always agree with us. Q: Your book emphasizes the value of “productive struggle.” You write, “Struggle doesn’t mean you’re suffering.” Instead, we get a handle on things by struggling to learn them.  A: We need to recast how we think about struggle, as something that is formative rather than a problem to be solved. I draw a lot of parallels in the book between some of the societal changes that occurred post-industrialization, when suddenly people no longer needed to be physically active to be economically productive. We saw more people suddenly develop physical exercise as something we do intentionally, that required reframing of what physical struggle meant. And I think we need that sort of shift about what we think about cognitive struggle.  Q: Given all this, what can we do to maintain some reasonable level of cognitive effort today? A: At the personal level, I emphasize four principles for navigating this age of AI. One is embracing the struggle, as we’ve talked about. The second rule is: Value who you are without AI. I’ve seen so many presentations over the last couple of years where someone has put together this very polished-looking presentation with Claude, but when they present it, it’s clear they didn’t put in the work necessary to understand the material. The formative struggle creates what I refer to as an “inseparable task bundle,” since making the slides allows me to engage in substantive discussion. In the absence of valuing who you are without AI, we get the product, but not the ability to capitalize on it. The third rule is about reinvesting your cognitive surplus. There are a lot of tasks for which AI can save you time — rote activities — but it matters what you do with those time savings. If you’re just funneling the same energy into the same tasks, you’re missing out on the potential transformational benefits of AI. The most innovative changes are not the ones that simply allow us to automate, but stretch the capabilities of  humanity in a productive way and build expertise. Or, people can channel that freed-up time to focus on family, learn a new language, cultivate skills.  The last rule is about using AI as your cognitive trainer. AI is this dual force, where it is very bad for thinking if you use it as an answer machine, but can be great for learning if you use it as a tutor. AI can be tailored to you. However, it requires that you seek out the friction of having a tutor, relative to having an answer machine. And that requires motivation.  This is a very challenging moment, and the problem is one we need to take seriously.
943c6910da212752: Di Malaysia, apa sahaja bisa menjadi isu politik. Termasuklah bahasa, sebagaimana tindakan sesetengah netizen cuba mengapi dan mengasapkan pemulauan terhadap rantaian kedai kopi (kopitiam) Oriental Kopi dengan alasan pelayannya kurang mahir berbahasa Melayu, selain menunya tidak cermat kerana tiada di dalam bahasa kebangsaan.
Selamat datang ke politik berbahasa di Malaysia. Apakah dimensi politik bahasa ini? Bagaimanakah cultural authority sedia ada bermain peranan?

Ketika menyampaikan titah diraja pada Istiadat Pembukaan Penggal Kelima Majlis Parlimen ke-15 di Parlimen pada 19 Jan 2026, Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim bertitah sebarang usaha untuk mengadakan sistem pendidikan baharu mesti dibuat selari dengan dasar pendidikan kebangsaan. Satu hal yang menonjol pada ucapan baginda itu adalah penegasan agar bahasa Melayu menjadi bahasa utama kerana ia adalah bahasa kebangsaan. "Oleh itu, sebarang usul untuk mengiktiraf apa juga sistem pendidikan lain mesti menerima bahasa Melayu dan sejarah Malaysia".

Isu ini bukanlah sederhana, ia membawa kita kembali kepada persoalan kewarganegaraan di mana bukan Melayu yang bersedia menerima identiti Malaysia perlu menerima pula bahasa Melayu sebagai bahasa rasmi, mestilah boleh dan bersedia bertutur dalam bahasa tersebut. Titah Sultan Ibrahim tersebut tidak syak lagi merupakan singgungan mengenai isu berkait UEC (Sijil Peperiksaan Bersepadu).

UEC adalah peperiksaan berpusat yang dikendalikan oleh Sekolah Menengah Persendirian Cina (SMPC) di bawah Gabungan Persatuan Guru Sekolah Cina Malaysia (Jiao Zong). Ia bukanlah peperiksaan di bawah Kementerian Pendidikan dan tiada kaitan dengan Sekolah Jenis Kebangsaan Cina di bawah Kementerian Pendidikan. Kelemahan atau ketidakmampuan sebahagian besar pelajar berbangsa Cina menguasai bahasa Melayu bukanlah sesuatu yang terbina dari persepsi politik tetapi telah pun dibuktikan dalam pelbagai kajian akademik, antara lain oleh Ang Lay Hoon dan Che Radiah Mezah, menerusi makalah ilmiah 'Masalah Penggunaan Bahasa Melayu dalam Kalangan Pelajar Etnik Cina di Malaysia' pada tahun 2012.

Masyarakat Cina berusaha melobi parti-parti politik untuk mengiktiraf UEC. Mereka yang menyokong pengiktirafan UEC menegaskan ia adalah bahagian daripada hak asasi manusia, akses adil kepada pendidikan dan peluang kerjaya, dan sama sekali bukan satu ancaman kepada bahasa kebangsaan, iaitu bahasa Melayu. Isu ini ditunggang oleh ahli-ahli parti politik khusus dalam helah memomokkan kelompok masyarakat Cina yang dianggap gagal mengasimilasi kebudayaan kebangsaan. Manakala, kelompok kanan Melayu pula beranggapan ia sebagai satu ancaman dan sengaja mencabar Dasar Pendidikan Kebangsaan, di mana naratif yang diketengahkan adalah UEC tidak selari dengan Falsafah Pendidikan Kebangsaan memandangkan silibus sejarah dan bahasa pengantar di sekolah persendirian Cina ini menggunakan bahasa Mandarin.

Loke Siew Fook, setiausaha agung DAP, parti yang mendapat sokongan meluas pengundi berbangsa Cina berulang kali menyatakan bahawa sebahagian besar pelajar UEC menguasai bahasa Melayu dan mengambil peperiksaan Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) bagi memastikan kelayakan mereka menepati standard kebangsaan.

Untuk mengambil jalan tengah, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim menyatakan kerajaan tidak mengiktiraf sukatan pelajaran UEC secara rasmi, sebaliknya sekadar memberikan laluan bersyarat untuk kemasukan lulusan tertentu ke institusi pendidikan tinggi tempatan dengan syarat wajib lulus bahasa Melayu dan sejarah.

Bahasa Melayu adalah bahasa kebangsaan dan bahasa rasmi mengikut Perkara 152 Perlembagaan. Mana-mana pelajar UEC yang berhasrat memasuki universiti awam di Malaysia wajib memperoleh sekurang-kurangnya gred kepujian (kredit) dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu di peringkat SPM. Ini bagi memastikan mereka mempunyai kompetensi linguistik untuk berinteraksi dan berfungsi dalam ekosistem awam Malaysia.

Selain itu, pengetahuan tentang sejarah tanah air dianggap sebagai asas kepada pembentukan jati diri dan kesetiaan kepada negara. Oleh demikian lulus dalam mata pelajaran sejarah SPM dijadikan syarat wajib yang tidak boleh dikompromi. Ini bagi memastikan setiap mahasiswa di universiti awam, tanpa mengira latar belakang sekolah mereka, dapat berkongsi naratif sejarah watan yang sama.

Pada masa sama aktivis pendidikan yang objektif menggesa Persekutuan Persatuan Lembaga Pengurus Sekolah Cina Malaysia (Dong Zong) menunjukkan keterbukaan bagi membenarkan elemen-elemen sastera, geografi, dan sivik tempatan diintegrasikan ke dalam silibus mereka. Mereka berpandangan pengiktirafan bersifat dua hala; di mana pihak kerajaan juga berhak menuntut penyesuaian terhadap aspirasi nasional dan ia mesti dilaksanakan oleh pihak pengurusan UEC. Harapannya adalah menerusi pendekatan berhati-hati ini, kemasukan pelajar UEC ke universiti awam tidak menggugat Dasar Pendidikan Kebangsaan dan Dasar Kebudayaan Kebangsaan. Bahkan ia boleh bertindak sebagai instrumen integrasi sosial yang menarik mereka graduan Sekolah Persendirian Cina ke dalam arus perdana pembinaan negara.

Seruan Sultan Ibrahim di Dewan Rakyat adalah satu bentuk penegasan cultural authority. Sebagai seorang raja, ia bukanlah kali pertama baginda menekankan pandangan. Pada tahun 2015, baginda mengkritik sistem pendidikan yang menggunakan bahasa Melayu, Mandarin dan Tamil yang dianggapnya menghalang penguasaan bahasa Melayu. Kritikan ini diulang lagi ketika baginda sudah menjadi Agong, di mana baginda menyatakan kehairanan mengapa masih ada rakyat Malaysia tidak boleh berbahasa Melayu, sambil menggesa agar sistem pendidikan negara menjadikan sistem pendidikan sekolah di peringkat rendah hanya satu aliran.

Isu kemampuan menguasai bahasa kebangsaan ini sudah tentu menjadi bahan rangup untuk kumpulan kanan Melayu, di mana penegasan terhadap kebudayaan kebangsaan yang berteraskan bangsa Melayu dipasakkan kembali. Gepena, yang merupakan gabungan kumpulan penulis berbahasa Melayu misalnya pernah mengambil kesempatan dengan meminta aktivis pendidikan Cina tunduk kepada kebudayaan kebangsaan yang berteraskan bangsa dan bahasa Melayu.

Tokoh kanan, dan Timbalan Presiden Muafakat Nasional, Ridhuan Tee Abdullah misalnya mengambil peluang ketidakmampuan graduan sekolah-sekolah Cina persendirian dan keengganan mereka untuk meningkatkan jam pembelajaran bahasa Melayu di sekolah sebagai satu keingkaran, dan mengisyaratkan agar kerajaan menggunakan kuasa dan kekerasan untuk membolehkan bahasa Melayu menjadi keutamaan. Ridhuan juga sering mengkritik papan tanda jalan yang tidak menggunakan bahasa kebangsaan. Dalam satu insiden yang melucukan tetapi dapat menggambarkan bagaimana cultural authority sering dipertengkar dan dipolitikkan, Ridhuan meminta sepanduk Hungry Ghost Festival yang disambut oleh masyarakat Cina ditulis dalam bahasa Melayu.

Selain manipulasi isu bahasa Melayu dalam bidang pendidikan yang ditunggang kumpulan dan tokoh kanan demi menunjukkan kejaguhan masing-masing; bahasa Melayu juga dijadikan bahan politik, untuk tujuan sama. Sebagai contoh, pada tahun 2025, dalam satu skandal sukan yang menyebabkan tujuh pemain antarabangsa digantung Fifa selama 12 bulan kerana memalsukan dokumen berkait status warisan, PAS menggunakan skandal tersebut untuk menjadikan Menteri Dalam Negeri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail sebagai sasaran.

Kerajaan Malaysia mendakwa seramai 23 pemain bola sepak telah diberi taraf kewarganegaraan Malaysia melalui proses naturalisasi sejak tahun 2018, dan ini termasuklah tujuh pemain warisan tersebut. Semua kelulusan ini dibuat mengikut peruntukan undang-undang serta Perlembagaan. Menteri dalam negeri seterusnya berhujah yang setiap permohonan diproses mengikut Perkara 19 Perlembagaan dan Kaedah-kaedah Warganegara yang menetapkan tiga syarat utama iaitu pemohon mesti bermastautin di Malaysia, berkelakuan baik serta mempunyai pengetahuan mencukupi dalam bahasa Melayu. Jawatankuasa Tatatertib Persekutuan Bola Sepak Antarabangsa (Fifa) mengenakan hukuman terhadap Persatuan Bolasepak Malaysia (FAM) dan tujuh pemain ini kerana melanggar Artikel 22 Kod Tatatertib Fifa berkaitan pemalsuan dokumen. Antara pemain terlibat ialah Gabriel Felipe Arrocha, Facundo Tomás Garcés, Rodrigo Julián Holgado, Imanol Javier Machuca, João Vitor Brandão Figueiredo, Jon Irazábal Iraurgui dan Hector Alejandro Hevel Serrano.

Ketua Penerangan PAS Fadhli Shaari dalam usaha memanjangkan skandal ini, dan untuk memerangkap menteri dalam negeri mencabar agar satu video ringkas tujuh pemain naturalisasi berbahasa Melayu disiarkan, memandangkan pengetahuan asas tentang bahasa itu adalah antara syarat wajib memperolehi kewarganegaraan. fd86b99ff025c2e8: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s call for Malaysia and Egypt to expand educational cooperation beyond Islamic studies is strategically sound.
Indeed, it should be understood as part of a larger effort to strengthen Malaysia’s geopolitical depth in the Middle East and North Africa.
Egypt is not merely a centre of Islamic civilisation.
It is one of the nine pivotal states whose affairs can affect the whole region — not unlike Algeria, Turkey, Indonesia, Pakistan, India, South Africa, Brazil and Mexico.
It is a massive Arab and African power whose geography, diplomatic influence and control of the Suez Canal make it indispensable to international trade and regional security.
President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi’s state visit to Malaysia on Oct 10, 2026, is more than just another diplomatic exchange.
It offers both countries an opportunity to elevate their longstanding relationship into a comprehensive strategic partnership.

Anwar’s emphasis on engineering, medicine, electrical and electronics, artificial intelligence and digital technology reflects an appreciation that modern diplomacy must combine intellectual cooperation with economic and technological capabilities.
Al-Azhar University will remain central to Malaysia’s religious and educational relationship with Egypt.
Its intellectual tradition of moderation, or “wasatiyyah”, continues to provide an important foundation for Islamic scholarship.
Yet bilateral cooperation cannot remain confined to religious education when the geopolitical environment surrounding both countries has become increasingly complicated.
Malaysia needs strategic depth beyond Southeast Asia.

This means cultivating durable relationships with countries capable of providing diplomatic access, economic opportunities, technological collaboration and strategic understanding across several regions.
Egypt offers precisely such an opportunity.
Situated at the intersection of Africa, especially the Horn of Africa, Mediterranean and the Middle East, Egypt occupies a geographical position that few countries can replicate.
Its control of the Suez Canal gives Cairo enormous strategic relevance.
The canal connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, making it one of the world’s most important maritime passages.
For Malaysia, whose economy depends heavily on international trade, disruptions along this corridor can produce serious consequences.
The Red Sea cannot be understood separately from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects it to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
Persistent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against maritime traffic have demonstrated how non-state actors can threaten international shipping, insurance costs and energy security.
Further east, the Strait of Hormuz remains another critical maritime chokepoint through which substantial quantities of global oil and liquefied natural gas move.

Although Egypt does not control either Bab el-Mandeb or Hormuz, its diplomatic networks and proximity to the Red Sea make it an important partner in understanding these interconnected vulnerabilities.
Malaysia must therefore develop a more sophisticated strategic appreciation of the Middle East and North Africa, the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz.
Such understanding cannot be acquired through occasional diplomatic visits alone.
It requires sustained cooperation among universities, maritime institutions, defence establishments, intelligence analysts and diplomatic academies.
Joint research on maritime security, supply-chain resilience, energy transportation and regional conflict management would provide immediate benefits.
Malaysia and Egypt could establish specialised academic programmes examining how instability in West Asia affects Southeast Asian economies.
Their universities could also cooperate in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, medicine, semiconductor technologies and renewable energy.
These initiatives would help transform educational exchanges into instruments of long-term strategic capacity.
The economic foundations are also already strengthening.
Malaysia could use Egypt as a gateway into African and Mediterranean markets, while Egypt could benefit from Malaysia’s established industrial networks and connections throughout Asean.
Both countries should also deepen defence dialogue, particularly in maritime awareness, military education and professional training.
This need not imply a military alliance. Strategic partnerships can strengthen resilience without creating unnecessary security obligations.
Malaysia’s foreign policy has traditionally emphasised non-alignment, constructive engagement and Asean centrality.
Closer cooperation with Egypt would complement rather than contradict these principles.
Indeed, Asean’s strategic interests increasingly extend beyond its immediate geographical boundaries.
Disruptions in the Red Sea or Hormuz can affect Malaysian manufacturers, exporters, consumers and energy markets.
Geographical distance no longer guarantees economic insulation.
The proposed Malaysia-Egypt strategic partnership should consequently be measured not by ceremonial declarations but by tangible institutional achievements.
Joint research centres, student exchanges, investment projects, maritime dialogues and coordinated diplomatic initiatives would demonstrate genuine progress.
Ultimately, Malaysia and Egypt possess complementary strengths.

Egypt offers geographical centrality, diplomatic experience and access to Africa and the Arab world. Malaysia contributes technological capabilities, industrial experience and connectivity to Southeast Asia.

By moving decisively beyond Islamic studies while preserving their historical educational bonds, both countries can construct a partnership capable of navigating an increasingly uncertain international order.
For Malaysia, strategic depth in the Middle East and North Africa is no longer a diplomatic luxury. It is becoming a geopolitical necessity.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
02a66f5cbb6850a8: In a previous column, I had argued that the Sedition Act 1948 ought to be struck down unless Parliament amends the Federal Constitution to expressly incorporate it as a permitted restriction on free speech.
As recently as in August, the prime minister himself called for this colonial-era law to be repealed to truly give meaning to Malaysia’s independence.
The fact that the remarks were made at a Merdeka event in UiTM was not lost on me. After all, his Pakatan Harapan coalition has also long championed the cause.
Despite that, to date, no action has been taken by our political leaders to fulfil this pledge.
That has kept the draconian law, which significantly curtails freedom of speech, on the statute books well past its expiry date, and still available for use against ordinary citizens.

Perhaps, our politicians have other priorities presently— or maybe they have no incentive to push the necessary bill to repeal the law. The Dewan Rakyat may be in session, but its present focus is the supply bill to fund the government for 2027.

So what recourse does the rakyat have? The attorney-general (AG), being the guardian of public interest, could move a motion in the Federal Court asking for the Act to be struck down. However, his silence thus far suggests that that item is nowhere on his agenda.
Will the Bar Council, an NGO, activists or a member of the public pick the matter up? No one knows.
Yet, as I have consistently maintained, the courts possess ample constitutional authority to move the dial given the inertia shown by our elected representatives.

In my view the jurisprudence related to oath of office and constitutional judicial power read with Article 4 is ripe enough for the legal community to bring forth strategic constitutional challenges before the relevant courts, including by inviting the court to exercise its suo motu powers.

The oath of office, which binds judges to “preserve, protect and defend” the constitutional rights of all Malaysians, imposes upon the courts a sacred duty not merely to safeguard those rights, but to actively facilitate their empowerment.

In my view, the process should involve very little red tape. Following the practice in India, a letter to the High Court or the Federal Court should be sufficient to set the wheels of justice in motion—since the judicial power invoked is exercised directly according to the oath of office and not under Article 121(1).

However, the courts should not act on its own. It should invite the AG, the Malaysian Bar, the Advocates Association of Sarawak, and the Sabah Law Society to weigh in on whether the Sedition Act can truly coexist within the constitutional supremacy regime.
No one can accuse the courts of going rogue, especially since our political leaders have already expressed publicly an intention to do the very same thing.
So, will the legal industry make an attempt?
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
cef6d0807cbc1074: The Budget 2027 allocation for the health ministry (MOH) and public healthcare has been raised to RM47.7bil, only RM1.2 billion extra which is the smallest increase in five years.
This falls well short of the Pakatan Harapan election promise to target 5% of GDP for public sector health expenditure in terms of both money and percentage.
At 10.3% of the total federal budget and 2.1% of GDP, the budget for the MOH has hardly changed in the last five years.

This shows that it is still “business as usual” in terms of public sector health expenditure and the small increase in the ministry’s budget barely exceeds the general inflation rate let alone medical inflation.

The government has met its longstanding promise to solve the issue of contract doctors and must be given credit for that. Anwar claims that MOH will create more than 9,000 vacancies to absorb the current contract doctors and newly trained housemen.
The allocation for the number of positions shows this, and the promise that new batches of trained housemen will be appointed directly to permanent positions is likely to be kept.

This demonstrates that coordination with the public service department (JPA) and the political will to solve the position problem through planning can be effective. It has taken more than a decade, but better late than never.
The new medical officers looking to serve in the public sector are still looking for higher pay, flexibility in appointments and job security.

The increase to the incentives for nurses and paramedics is only RM100 per month and does little to address concerns about low pay compared to peers in the private sector and overseas, such as in Singapore and the Middle East.
Brain drain is considered severe; this budget policy announcement is only a small, welcome adjustment and does not address the systemic issue of staff retention.
The realisation that more ambulances are needed for effective emergency care and the decision to purchase additional ambulances is a welcome change in management.
Nonetheless, there still are too many gaps in the public healthcare system.
With this small budget increase and without complementary policies and the necessary political will, these issues will not be resolved.
Some of these issues are not about money at all. They are about management and changing old-style human resource processes.

On the other hand, spending for public-private healthcare has increased from RM144 million to RM200 million for next year. This is a substantial increase for the outsourcing of public sector patients to the private sector.

An earlier government report stated that RM66.5 million was spent on 24,000 outsourced patients. If the government can maintain this rate, it could free up more than 70,000 public sector patients next year.
While this would improve waiting times in public hospitals, it would probably have only a minimal impact compared to the estimated 19 million outpatient visits in 2024.
However, for certain medical treatments and procedures, this could have a meaningful impact on waiting times.
With the Hospital Services Outsourcing Programme now covering 14 specialty areas, the increase in allocation will be welcome news for public sector patients but it is a form of privatisation.

The policy announcement regarding MediAsas and price transparency in private healthcare is also a form of privatisation and likely to have a greater impact on access to care and help to keep medical inflation in check.
While these might not require significant budget allocation from the government, the government will certainly need to step up its regulatory efforts.
This is the real challenge. If healthcare is to be balanced between public and private providers, then regulation and management must improve.
I would like to thank Dr Lim Chee Han for his valuable insights.

54f95897dfd35ce6: Dalam artikel ini saya ingin mengulas tulisan sahabat saya A Kathirasen berjudul Poets, Philosophers and Policy: The moral language of Budget 2027, yang mengupas bahasa falsafah, puisi dan agama dalam belanjawan Anwar Ibrahim. Mesej artikel tersebut adalah bacaan penulis sendiri betapa Anwar cuba memberi suatu mesej ‘kemanusiaan sejagat’ dalam terjemahan fiskal dan angka-angka wang ringgit dalam alokasi-alokasi masing-masing.

Kathirasen ingin menarik perhatian kepada asas bahawa belanjawan adalah aspek kematangan kemanusiaan, bukan semata-mata wang kocek di sini dan sana untuk dihabiskan. Penulis veteran itu juga ingin mengkiaskan usaha Anwar untuk mensejagatkan isu keperluan daripada pengasingan perkauman. Dalam artikel ini saya akan memanjangkan tafsiran Kathirasen dengan membawa mesej saya sendiri, iaitu, bahasa dan rujukan yang digunakan membawa konsep pemerintahan dan penjagaan negara memerlukan suatu bahasa Melayu-global.

Ada dua aspek yang ingin saya sentuh tentang penggunaan rujukan pelbagai kaum dan agama serta pelbagai sumber ketamadunan manusia dari kitab suci agama, kepada falsafah pemikir dan puisi pujangga. Pertama adalah tuduhan ‘liberal’ kepada sesiapa Melayu Muslim yang menggunakan sumber pemikiran atau falsafah dan refleksi spiritual daripada selain sumber Islam.
Keduanya adalah apakah yang saya maksudkan sebagai bahasa lingua franca Melayu global sebagai hamparan kepada pemikiran Anwar sebagai intelek Melayu-Islam.

Yang pertama adalah tuduhan yang selalu diajukan kepada sesiapa yang membawa argumen atau perbahasan atau konsep daripada pemikiran, refleksi dan falsafah dari selain Islam Sunni akan membawa tuduhan ‘liberal’ dan merosakkan serta menyesatkan orang Islam. Sebagai seorang ilmuan seni bina, saya amat memahami keperluan menggunakan sumber-sumber konsep, pemikiran dan prinsip-prinsip seni bina dari Barat seperti pemikiran Frank Lloyd Wright, Louis Sullivan, William Morris, Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe dan Le Corbusier. Sumber-sumber falsafah dan pemikiran dari Amerika Syarikat, England, Perancis dan Jerman amat perlu saya garapkan dalam memikir semula teori atau prinsip seni bina Islam, seni bina Malaysia dan seni bina Melayu moden.

Peminjaman pemikiran dari sumber luar atau lain dari kaum dan agama kita sendiri bukan bermaksud mengagungkan atau mengkiblatkan Barat atau Timur tetapi memberi pengiktirafan bahawa bangsa-bangsa manusia yang lain melalui pemodenan dan kesedaran dalam tahap yang berbeza serta waktu yang lebih awal dari kita di Malaysia. Arus revolusi industri meranapkan hubungan masyarakat dan pemerintah serta pemikiran ‘enlightenment’ pula mencabar tafsiran kehidupan, kosmos dan geografi duni daripada hanya interpretasi gereja sahaja.

Negara kita di rantau ini, walaupun mempunyai segala macam telefon pintar, AI, serta teknologi baharu yang terkini masih melalui suatu pertembungan antara pemikiran sains, politik dan agama yang telah dilalui orang di Barat dunia lebih 200 tahun sebelumnya.

Kita Melayu sampai lewat sikit. Maka itu penggunaan serta peminjaman konsep, istilah dan pemikiran daripada selain Islam menggambarkan keupayaan seorang Melayu menggarap dan membentuk suatu belanjawan yang bernyawakan moral, wawasan jauh dan ketamadunan kemanusiaan.

Belanjawan negara adalah bukan semata-mata belanjawan korporat yang tahu untung rugi sahaja. Maka itu adalah tidak wajar pada sesiapa yang akan menuding jari “nah itu bunyi orang Melayu-Islam liberal” ataupun “nah itu bunyi orang yang dijajah pemikiran kolonial dari Barat dan dari sumber musuh Islam”.

Sebagai ilmuan, semua para cerdik pandai tahu bahawa kebenaran merentasi kaum dan agama kerana kaum dan agama yang difahami itu telah disempitkan oleh golongan yang disuruh menjaga integriti warisan tersebut. Namun demikian, penjaga warisan ugama yang berpendidikan tidak pelbagai disiplin dan ilmu hanya dapat melihatnya dengan satu belah teropong sahaja.

Perkara kedua adalah bagaimana Anwar memainkan peranan seorang Melayu global dan bukan Melayu-parti atau Melayu-ustaz. Untuk menjadi suatu bangsa yang berjaya, orang Melayu perlu mengetahui pelbagai sumber pemikiran yang datang dari pelbagai bangsa dan budaya. Seperti juga Hang Tuah yang telah memohon ayahandanya untuk beliau mempelajari lebih daripada 10 bahasa asing. Melayu yang mempunyai akses kepada pemikiran daripadapelbagai sumber lain tidak akan terbantut kepada retorik perpaduan Melayu untuk kuasa serta kesucuan agama tanpa kematangan global dan menyeluruh. Saya sering mengajar pelajar PhD bahawa semua ilmu adalah tafsiran orang yang hendak menggunakannya pada ketika itu dan dalam konteks kefahaman teknologi, sains dan budaya manusia selainnya sahaja. Maka, sesuatu ilmu seperti ilmu agama boleh diperluaskan atau diperkecilkan mengikut kehendak seseorang. Ilmu perlu melimpah kepada pemikiran dan tafsiran setiap masa berubah dan juga perubahan untuk berpindah kerana situasi semasa.

Akhir sekali, saya mencadangkan janganlah kita terlalu pantas menghukum ‘sesat’ atau ‘liberal’ kepada sesiapa hanya kerana mereka menggunakan istilah luar yang kita sendiri tidak tahu hujung pangkal. Perkara pokok yang perlu dijiwai daripada artikel saya dan Kathirasen adalah belanjawan bukan semata-mata angka yang diagih-agihkan kepada semua kememterian. Seperkara lagi adalah penggunaan istilah, konsep dan falsafah yang merentasi jurang kaum, agama dan budaya adalah keupayaan berfikir luar daripada kepompong tradisi. Hanya dengan percampuran dan menjunamkan diri ke dalam budaya lain maka barulah kita boleh menggarap solusi baharu serta arah tuju sama yang cekal dan kental.

972ce96df38a5766: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.

Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.

The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)

02ae3f5fc0dc9f97: It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships.

Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security.

To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day.
378737ffe80d7a1a: In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages. If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers, and emergency response officials around the globe. A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition. In a new paper in Nature, the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks. “Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says. “It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.”  Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft. Longer forecasts In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes. “He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says. “That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that.” Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models, which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they’re even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges. Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. “That range is referred to as the ‘predictability desert,’ because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone’s focused on this winter,” Cohen says. “The subseasonal range can’t take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice.” Cohen credits his co-author Lester Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models. “We built this wrapper — Lester calls it postprocessing,” Cohen says. “We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them.” While other forecasting systems do more simplistic error correction, the research team’s postprocessing layer uses AI to learn from a forecasting system’s mistakes based on historic data and shifts its forecasts. In that time range, forecasters use so-called probabilistic forecasts, where the likelihood of a range of possibilities if given. “As more forecasts and data become available, our model adaptively improves its correction,” Cohen says. To build the model, the researchers used MIT Engaging, a supercomputing cluster hosted by MIT’s Office of Research Computing and Data, but the resulting model does not require a supercomputer to run. To put their model to the test, last year the research team submitted three models that included their post-processing layer to the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is considered the best forecasting center in the world. Each season ECMWF holds forecasting competitions between models. The submission that won first place combined ECMWF’s forecasting model with another, and then applied the postprocessing correction on top. That approach ended up doubling the original model’s predictive power in the subseasonal range. For the first time, the model offered an improvement over relying on climatologic averages. “Up until now, no one had been able to show a model predicts weather better than long term averages for these subseasonal forecasts,” Cohen says. “They’ve pretty much all been worse than that — you could literally flip a coin and do better. People have questioned if it’s even worth investing in models at all for this time range. We consistently beat climatology averages with our models.” The model also showed a statistically significant improvement in the ability to predict extreme weather. “That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish,” Cohen says. “When the ECMWF developed their own, non-AI, error-correction to their model, it got worse at predicting extreme weather. I think that’s because traditional error, or bias, correction is always trying to get to the mean, whereas extreme weather is on the fringe of probabilities.” Preparing for disaster In the Nature paper, the team showed their technique could be used to improve land forecasts in most regions across the globe. They also applied their bias correction technique to other models and showed it improved those as well, putting even lesser models on par with the ECMWF’s forecasts. “What’s nice about our model is it’s an add-on wrapper,” Cohen explains. “We used it with the ECMWF’s dynamical model because that was considered the best, but it can be used with any model. It even improves models that are already bias corrected using another AI algorithm. So it shows a robust improvement. And it’s open source and low cost.” Cohen says the meteorological office for the Republic of Kenya has already reached out about implementing the model to improve forecasting of the annual monsoon season to improve agricultural yields this winter. He hopes other groups will also use the model. “This could help you decide when to fertilize around rain, when there’s a freeze coming to protect crops during winter harvests, or help you avoid droughts,” Cohen says. “It could also be useful for energy and emergency management. I’ve talked to energy officials who say, ‘If I’m told two days before that an ice storm’s coming, I don’t have enough time, but if I had two weeks, that could be enough to make adequate preparations.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support, and the European Union.
