f906b803e3fa3d76: Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Budget 2027 address did not disappoint, transforming fiscal data into an intellectual narrative, and breathing life into the ledger by anchoring it in philosophy.

In tabling the Supply Bill on Oct 9, he assembled a jury of philosophers, poets, and thinkers from five civilisations and asked them to testify. He sought their assistance in telling Malaysians that a budget is not merely arithmetic but a covenant—and that covenants are owed to the future. Everything else in the speech is scaffolding around that claim.
Anwar opened with lighad (“for tomorrow”) from Surah al-Hashr (59:18), establishing intergenerational obligation as a religious duty before it becomes a fiscal one.

He said: “True progress is measured not by how far we travel, but by what we carry together along the way: human dignity, strong families, a fair chance for each generation to rise, the integrity of our institutions, and the conviction that effort will be repaid with opportunity. It is not enough to inherit our strengths. We must enlarge them, until they become a greater legacy for those who follow.”
He then introduced British philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s hedgehog and the fox image: a nation needs "one big thing" held steadily (its ambition) and many things known flexibly (its methods).
“The fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing. A nation needs both. A nation must hold to one great and constant ambition: a purpose that gives the journey its direction and meaning.”
Immediately after, tenth-century jurist Al-Mawardi established that power cannot stand without order, law, and responsibility.
This was paired with the classical Malay poet Raja Ali Haji’s Gurindam Dua Belas (1847), anchoring the bond between ruler and ruled in waad—a covenant.

“In our tradition, the bond between those who govern and those who are governed has never rested on power alone. It is anchored in waad – a covenant, in which loyalty must be answered with justice, and power must be fenced in by trust.”

The American philosopher John Rawls then performed the heaviest analytical lifting, deploying it at exactly the right moment. After announcing differentiated allocations to states, Anwar anticipated accusations of favouritism and relied on equity rather than uniform treatment:

"That is how we have approached allocations to the states. Developed states can keep surging ahead. Developing states get room to pick up the pace... That is what equity means: not every state getting the same, but every state getting what is fair and reasonable."

Although invoking Rawlsian-adjacent logic provided a philosophical wrapper for inter-governmental distribution, applying it directly glossed over the complex constitutional debates of federal funding formulas. Yet, the rhetoric served its purpose.

Next, Tamil poet-philosopher Thiruvalluvar’s Thirukkural (couplet 731)—which describes a good country as having adequate food production, learned citizens and honest businessmen - arrived just before a RM69 billion education allocation, including RM50 million for Tamil primary schools.
Likewise, a Tang-dynasty monk's verse (Shangtang Kaishi Song) on the plum blossom enduring bitter cold was placed right before fiscal sacrifice and subsidy rationalisation were addressed.
Homer closed the arc. Odysseus braves storms yet never loses his unwavering memory of Ithaca:
"Every nation must know its Ithaca: the ambition it seeks, the values and roots it will defend, and the legacy it means to leave."
Anwar returned to lighad at the close, sealing the ring.

This was no random name-dropping. It was a deliberate comparative theology of governance. Anwar treated the Quran, the Tirukkural, Homer, and Rawls not as conflicting authorities, but as different dialects of the same moral language.

Justice, foresight, and institutional integrity were framed not as Western, Islamic, Indian, Chinese, or Malay monopolies, but as universal human aspirations - a potent message for a multi-ethnic society.
By framing fiscal decisions through a civilisational lens, Anwar attempted to elevate fiscal discipline from a technical necessity to a moral imperative.

One might be tempted to see this as an effort to depoliticise the budget but that risks oversimplifying domestic realpolitik. Rather than neutralising politics, the rhetoric attempted to reshape the terms of political engagement, lifting the conversation above mere transactional patronage.
Anwar’s rhetoric was undeniably ambitious. He wanted Malaysians to see the budget as the fulfillment of a shared moral contract.
Yet, a tension remains.
The intention is to unify, but the ultimate success depends on whether economic benefits are tangibly felt across all communities.

In the end, this covenant will not be weighed in the Dewan Rakyat, but in the lives of the rakyat. If this pluralist vision translates into equitable prosperity, Anwar’s citations will be remembered as the blueprint for a new Malaysia. If not, they will be seen as just beautiful words without substance.

13096602de9f3aae: From Boo Jia Cher
The chaos at Sepang International Circuit during the Formula 1 weekend was frustrating, but hardly surprising.

Thousands of fans were left stranded. Crowds spilled onto the highway, with some fans walking along emergency lanes towards Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Shuttle buses struggled to cope with the sudden surge, while traffic around the circuit ground to a standstill.
It would be easy to dismiss this as a one-off failure of event management. But for anyone who uses Malaysian public transport every day, the problems at Sepang should look very familiar.
Sepang was simply a much bigger, more visible version of the transport problems we already face in our cities.
We still don't take buses seriously
At the heart of the problem is a basic mistake in how we design our roads: buses are still treated as a mode of transport that has to squeeze into traffic, rather than being given priority.
Whenever a major event is expected to attract large crowds, the usual solution is simple: add more buses.

However, putting more buses onto the same congested roads does not solve much. A bus is only useful if it can actually move. A 12-metre bus carrying 50 or 60 people has little advantage over dozens of cars if it is stuck in the same traffic.
That is what happened at Sepang. Once the roads around the circuit became jammed, the shuttle buses could not bypass the congestion. They became part of it.

If a bus that normally takes 20 minutes to complete a trip takes two hours instead, the number of passengers it can carry over the course of the day collapses. Adding more buses only helps if there is enough road capacity for them to move.

This is the same problem commuters face every morning on roads such as Jalan Ampang and the Federal Highway. You can see buses sitting in the same three-lane traffic jam as everyone else while carrying dozens of passengers who chose public transport to avoid sitting in traffic.

A bus carrying 50 people should not have to compete for road space with 50 separate cars. If we want buses to work, they need dedicated, physically protected bus lanes that cannot simply become another lane for cars whenever traffic gets bad.
Grab is not mass transit

Another problem is the tendency to lump taxis and e-hailing services such as Grab into the same category as public transport. They are useful, of course. But they are not a substitute for mass transit.

A Grab car still occupies roughly the same road space as any other car. And when tens of thousands of people leave an event at roughly the same time, asking each person to book an individual car creates an enormous amount of traffic.
Cars have to queue to pick people up, stop at roadsides, make U-turns and squeeze through already crowded roads.

One bus can carry dozens of people in a single vehicle. To move the same number of passengers using individual cars requires a long line of vehicles. That difference matters enormously when road space is limited.

Instead of using e-hailing as a substitute for public transport, planners should treat it as a feeder service that helps people get to rail stations and bus hubs, rather than something that replaces high-capacity transport altogether. Otherwise, we end up filling our roads with hundreds of low-capacity vehicles precisely when we need to move the most people.
The problem doesn't stop at Sepang
There is another problem that is easier to miss. Where do all those extra buses and drivers come from?

In an already underserved public transport system, buses and drivers have to be pulled from regular routes to serve major events. That means someone elsewhere can end up waiting longer for a bus simply because another part of the country is hosting a major event.

This is a sign of how little spare capacity our bus networks have. A healthy public transport system should have enough buses and drivers to handle a major event without effectively robbing one to pay another.
A weekend transport surge can put pressure on ordinary commuters in surrounding neighbourhoods. People who had nothing to do with the event can end up paying for it through longer waiting times.
Johor Bahru should take note

Sepang should also be a warning for Johor Bahru. The upcoming RTS Link will bring large numbers of passengers directly into Bukit Chagar and central Johor Bahru. The rail connection itself is a major and potentially transformative investment.
However, trains do not exist in isolation. What happens after passengers leave the station matters just as much.

If thousands of commuters step out from the Bukit Chagar station and find themselves surrounded by cars, taxis and e-hailing vehicles fighting for space on already congested roads, we could end up recreating the same problem as Sepang, but every day.

Johor Bahru also has a basic problem with walkability. Walking between Bukit Chagar and nearby parts of the city can still mean dealing with broken pavements, a lack of shade, missing crossings and wide, intimidating roads.

A person should not need a car just to cross the street or walk a few hundred metres from a train station. If walking is unpleasant and buses are stuck in traffic, many people will simply choose to drive or book a Grab instead. That adds even more cars to the streets around the station.

The RTS can bring huge numbers of people into the city, but the city still needs to give those people somewhere to go. That means proper pedestrian connections, safe crossings, shaded walkways and dedicated bus lanes should be treated as part of the RTS investment, not as optional improvements to be dealt with later.
We cannot traffic-manage our way out of this

The response to the Sepang chaos focused heavily on traffic police, lane diversions and managing the flow of vehicles. Those things have their place, but they cannot solve a more fundamental problem: too many people are being asked to use the same limited road space at the same time.

We need to start designing our roads around how many people they can move, rather than how many cars they can accommodate. That means giving buses and other high-capacity vehicles priority on dedicated lanes.

It means managing e-hailing pick-up points so they do not clog the entrances to major transport hubs. Major events should also have enough dedicated transport capacity without stripping ordinary neighbourhood bus routes, while walking and cycling should be made a realistic part of the journey, especially around major train stations.

For one weekend, Sepang gave us an unusually clear view of a problem that normally plays out more quietly across Malaysian cities: we built our roads around cars, then expected public transport to somehow work within them.
The lesson from Sepang will keep repeating itself on our highways, outside our train stations, and on the daily commute home, as long as we don't fundamentally change our transport planning.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

e3df02bdb07de425: “We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.” So begins the UN Charter. Yet Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is well into its fourth year, confirming just how far the UN has strayed from its foundational promise.

The problem is not simply that the UN has failed to stop a major war. It is that the state waging the war exercises a veto within the very body that the Charter entrusts with preserving international peace and security.

Last month, the Security Council met once again to discuss Ukraine, and once again, the world saw how Russia has turned the Soviet Union’s permanent seat, which it usurped in 1991, into a license for impunity. If ever the council tries to respond to Russian aggression, the Kremlin blocks it.

This perverse arrangement is usually described as an unfortunate but unavoidable flaw of the system. But is it? The UN has never examined how the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) or its successor, the Russian Federation, acquired membership in the organisation and on the Security Council in the first place.
Yet surely this matter warrants closer scrutiny. On the basis of which documents, exactly, did Russia inherit the Soviet Union’s veto-wielding position?
The answer is remarkably thin. Article 23 of the Charter still lists the “Union of Soviet Socialist Republics” as a permanent member of the Security Council.
The Soviet Union was a founding member of the UN in 1945, as were Ukraine (UkSSR) and Belarus (BSSR). The same cannot be said for the RSFSR or the Russian Federation.

To be sure, on Dec 8, 1991, Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine declared that the Soviet Union was ceasing to exist “as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality”; and on Dec 21, in Alma-Ata (now Almaty), the members of the new Commonwealth of Independent States, including Ukraine, expressed support for Soviet Russia’s continuation of the USSR’s UN membership, including its permanent seat on the Security Council.

But then no legal steps were taken to secure this status ever. Instead, on Dec 24, RSFSR president Boris Yeltsin sent the UN secretary-general a letter stating that the Soviet Union’s membership was being “continued” by the Russian Federation. But it is hard to assign legal weight to this letter, because no state called the Russian Federation existed when Yeltsin sent it.

Moreover, the UN Charter explains clearly what membership requires: a formal application, Security Council consideration, an assessment of compliance with Article 2, a recommendation to the General Assembly, deliberation and a vote in the assembly, parliamentary ratification of the Charter, and a deposit of the instrument of ratification with the designated authority. There is no evidence that Russia completed this process, or even attempted to begin it.

Russia’s usurpation of the Soviet seat has no comparable precedent in UN history. When the former Yugoslavia tried the same dubious manoeuvre in 1992, the Security Council (Resolution 777) unequivocally rejected its claim to be a continuing state.

Yet in December 2022, when Ukraine’s parliament and foreign ministry formally stated that Russia’s UN membership had never been properly established, the response was silence—a tacit admission that no one could offer a credible legal rebuttal.
The proper response is obvious. Russia should be stripped of the right to represent the Soviet Union, on grounds that it came to its permanent membership on the Security Council illegitimately.

Now that its usurpation of the Soviet Union’s rights has enabled it to wage a war of aggression, putting the political and legal questions of its membership on the agenda is crucial for upholding the UN’s core mission and securing punishment for the crimes against humanity committed as part of an attack on a UN member state.

The UN has at least two precedents to draw on here. The first is China. In 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognising the representatives of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as “the only legitimate representatives of China” and removing Chiang Kai-shek’s representatives. The vote was 76 to 35, with 17 abstentions. The PRC also assumed the permanent seat on the Security Council, though Article 23 was not amended (it still refers to the “Republic of China”).
The cases are not identical. In China’s case, two governments claimed to represent a state that continued to exist. But this distinction only strengthens the case for revisiting Russia’s status.
If deciding who represented an existing state required a vote, why was the question of who would inherit the seat of a vanished state settled by a letter?
The second precedent is Yugoslavia. Here, a state had broken apart, its largest remnant declared itself the continuing state, and the UN Security Council plainly said no.

This answer was given to Belgrade but never to Moscow—not for legal reasons, but for political ones. There were no arguments to support it, and the issue was simply never brought up for discussion. Yugoslavia had neither nuclear weapons nor designs on a permanent seat.

Against this backdrop, a third instrument has acquired renewed significance since 2022: Resolution 377 (V), known as “Uniting for Peace”. Adopted in 1950, it addresses situations in which a disagreement among permanent members prevents the Security Council from fulfilling its responsibilities.

On Feb 27, 2022, the council invoked this provision to adopt Resolution 2623 by 11 votes to one, with three abstentions, calling an emergency special session of the General Assembly. Since the decision was procedural, Russia could not veto it.

But this instrument has its limits. It bypasses Russia’s veto without questioning its right to occupy the seat from which it is cast. The General Assembly can identify Russia as an aggressor, reaffirm Ukraine’s territorial integrity, condemn annexation, and recommend mechanisms for accountability.
But those decisions are recommendations. Russia retains the power to paralyse the body whose decisions are binding, even though the legality of its presence in that body has never been established.

The debate over Russia’s status must therefore be separated from the seemingly hopeless debate over Security Council reform. There is no need to abolish the veto to challenge Russia’s use of it. There is no need to rewrite the Charter to ask whether Russia is entitled to powers the Charter assigns to the Soviet Union. There is not even a need for a separate resolution. The General Assembly already has a Credentials Committee, the mechanism through which the South African delegation’s credentials were rejected in 1974.

What will happen to the Security Council if the seat is left empty? Nothing. When the Soviet Union boycotted the council from January to August 1950, the council adopted its resolutions on Korea. An empty seat is not a veto.
Some may argue that even raising the question is dangerous. Whatever Russia has done, they will say, a nuclear power must remain inside the UN, and a channel of communication must stay open.

But reviewing Russia’s status would neither end diplomacy nor invalidate every Security Council decision adopted with Russia’s participation. The question is whether diplomacy should continue to rest on a legal fiction.

The General Assembly should do what it failed to do in 1991: formally examine the legality of the Russian Federation’s representation of the former Soviet Union. The answer need not be predetermined, but the question must finally be raised.
Member states can examine Yeltsin’s letter, the Alma-Ata papers, the practice of state succession, the Charter, the precedents of China and Yugoslavia, and three decades of subsequent practice.

Russia can present its case, others can present theirs, and the General Assembly can vote. That is how a rules-based international order should work. A nameplate does not confer the right to a seat at the table. The rules do.
Denys Shtilierman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, is co-founder of #unrussiaUN, the initiative group for expelling Russia from the United Nations.

11e83311a7c54e72: As artificial intelligence becomes more and more powerful, its ability to handle human-like tasks is undeniable. Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code. Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance. The question for many neuroscientists is: What can these machine systems teach them about how the brain learns? And what kinds of models are likely to be the most informative? In a paper published Oct. 9 in the journal PNAS, scientists at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research and K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer. They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery. With some simple instructions about how and when connections should change, a group of randomly connected units can reshape itself into an effective information-processing network, learning from the data it is trained on. Biological learning “Current AI technology is working very well, but it doesn’t necessarily use a learning algorithm that is used by the brain,” says Qianli Liao, a K. Lisa Yang ICoN Center Postdoctoral Fellow in the labs of MIT professors and McGovern Institure members Tomaso Poggio and Mark Harnett, and co-first author of the PNAS paper with MIT Research Scientist Liu Ziyin and graduate student Yulu Gan. Liao explains that engineers design the rules about how connections change as an artificial neural network processes training data and receives feedback about its mistakes.   When it comes to training AI to do its job, the approach is powerful. But Liao and his colleagues caution that networks designed in this way may not offer much insight into biological learning. “The brain doesn't have an external designer or architect,” Liao says. “The brain has to organize itself. And we need to know how simple rules are going to make the brain organize.” The rules that reshape neural connections as an animal learns may be different in different parts of the brain, or they may change as the brain becomes more mature. Neuroscientists are working to understand how those rules work and how they might be disrupted by aging or disease — a vital step toward developing new therapies and prevention strategies. Liao points to the development of brain-computer interfaces, which aim to restore communication when the brain’s language abilities are lost or let paralyzed patients control neuroprosthetic limbs, as one potential application. “None of these can work without knowing the rules behind neuron-neuron interactions,” he says. “That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections. Self-organized artificial learning Working with Poggio and Harnett, Liao, Ziyin, and Gan set out to develop and validate a self-organizing computational network capable of learning. Liao explained that the network’s structure begins with multiple layers of randomly interconnected neuron-like units. Within each layer, every neuron-like component is subject to the same rules about how connections should be adjusted. “They just interact with each other using that rule, and they develop some type of behavior,” he says. The team’s network implements the kind of simple rules thought to rewire brain circuits as humans and other animals learn from their experiences. In both the brain and the machine network, for example, “neurons that fire together wire together.” In other words, when two connected neurons are activated at the same time, the connection between them strengthens.  The team showed that a self-organizing network governed by rules like these can learn to recognize patterns and classify images. They explain that in their model, learning is enabled by self-assembling motifs that emerge according to simple rules, then serve as building blocks for functional circuits. As their network learned, these motifs reorganized themselves using an optimization strategy similar to the approach built into most modern machine learning systems, called gradient descent, in which connections are gradually adjusted in response to errors in order to improve performance. Most modern AI implements gradient descent through some form of the back-propagation algorithm, which neuroscientists say is unlikely to be used by the brain. The team compared its self-organizing network to networks designed to learn in this way and found that it performed at a similar level. Connecting brains and machines Poggio says finding a biological parallel to back-propagation could trigger significant progress in both AI and neuroscience.  “If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says. Liao says a self-organizing network does not necessarily learn the same way the brain does — but it’s a critical starting point for biological plausibility.  “Self-organization is the first high-level framework,” he says. “Once we are good with self-organization as a measure, then we can talk about next thing.” While the group’s main objective is better understanding the brain, Liao says that knowledge could ultimately improve machine learning systems, too, enabling engineers to develop networks that perform better or in more human-like ways.
8ad1969e4f569b40: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities. "We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state." Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership.  In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors. "The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer.  Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths.  Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature. During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD.  "There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state." In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base.  Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said. Scaling up biomanufacturing One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector. "BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. "It will bring together industry, academia, and government to transform ideas into scalable biological products, supporting a secure and competitive bioindustrial future."  The project responds to NSCEB's call for a national network of biomanufacturing scale-up facilities, a capacity currently missing in New England, according to Wack. The facility will offer shared equipment, infrastructure, and secure laboratory space to help bridge the "valley of death" between early-stage discovery and commercial- or defense-scale production. BioSHIELD's ready-built support networks will be key to overcoming technological and regulatory hurdles, helping innovators rapidly move capabilities to market or military use.  A coalition supporting the project includes Massachusetts Biomedical Initiatives, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant, and Lincoln Laboratory. It builds on a foundational effort in central Massachusetts funding the Massachusetts TechHubs program. At the event, Wack announced the coalition has signed a memorandum of understanding to formalize the partnership. Design workshops are scheduled to begin soon, ahead of funding and construction. Connecting AI and biotechnology Other discussions centered on the intersection of biotechnology and AI, another critical area for national security. Panelists represented Boston University, the University of Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Wyss Institute, and Phicil-itate Change. They discussed challenges in collecting and disseminating high-quality, AI-ready datasets and opportunities for AI to improve biomanufacturing and therapeutics.  Closing the event, Wack called for continued collaboration as the nation moves at speed and scale to stay at the forefront of biotechnology. "At Lincoln Laboratory, we've built a strong foundation in biotechnology for more than 25 years, and it's heartening to see this level of coordinated work taking shape. It resonates with so many of us who view biotechnology as both an economic and national security imperative," Wack said.
c11b8b011c289276: In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI.

Disney is willing to pay $20 million for “a non-exclusive perpetual license” of certain Character Technologies intellectual property, the chatbot maker said in a press release that did not go into much further detail on which assets Disney wanted.

f17adc20acb8f853: Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming. The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google's app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations.

Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.

Google's other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google's app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.
2bad0427cfe4e7d6: Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it's only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won't have full access.

Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon's capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model's advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it's so capable.

The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.
a2352b9071f96ed2: When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”

The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
bbe9efcd05754558: When government officials craft policies, there is often a comment period for public feedback. Lawmakers have long had to sort through fake feedback that is mass-produced in an effort to sway policy, but they’ve generally gotten used to detecting it. With, artificial intelligence, however, people can submit realistic-seeming comments, which are harder to dismiss as being fabrications with no person behind them. That’s just one way AI can be used to generate text and statements, in civic conversations, for which no one can be found to be answerable. This issue, among others, has caught the attention of Deb Roy, professor of media arts and sciences at MIT and director of the MIT Center for Constructive Communication (CCC). In a new essay published in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, titled, “Who stands behind the words?,” Roy calls for a renewed emphasis on responsibility in communication, asserting that even when AI is used to craft text, there needs to be accountability and “answerability.” Building better group dialogues to produce more public trust is a core part of the work of CCC. The group, along with Cortico, the closely affiliated nonprofit Roy co-founded, has helped facilitate group discussions on important issues in many situations — including civic meetings, schools, deliberative assemblies, and private organizations — and used tech tools, including AI, to help find themes among comments, and more. But the center also designs this process so that participants can check and override the tech-based output at each key step. Ultimately, a person is responsible for every public comment. MIT News spoke to Roy about the essay and the work of the center.  Q: You’ve identified this problem about the lack of accountability behind words that are generated by AI. When did you really first notice this? A: It came into focus when Chat-GPT [which is powered by a large language model, or LLM] launched. As for my own history with language models, my PhD work explored what we might now call PLMs — Puny Language Models — so I’m quite familiar with language models and have tracked the field’s rapid evolution. But Chat-GPT turned a corner. Two things changed at the same time: the depth of the model and its knowledge, and the way you could interact with it.  I became obsessed with trying to find the limits of what it could do. And I felt that no matter how hard I tried to stretch my arms around it, I couldn’t. I built my tenure case at MIT on language grounding — the idea that it’s not enough for an AI system to just process lots of words and other symbols. I believed that to understand what words mean, you actually need a physical body and life experiences as part of the process. So I revisited the philosophy-of-AI literature I had once been steeped in, which asks what fundamentally distinguishes the kind of system that large language models exemplify, in extraordinarily advanced form, from the kind of processing we humans engage in. I gave several presentations to my own graduate students trying to make the case that, even though AI seems so intelligent, it’s actually different in kind — and I could not convince them.  And I thought, I know the difference, but I’m having trouble convincing even myself of what it is. And that led me to ask, “Wait a minute: Is there someone or something that stands behind the words, a human responsible for what is being said?” That’s the thing this extraordinary new language machine doesn’t have.  Whether these systems genuinely understand language is actively debated. But even if you grant them all the comprehension you like, they still lack standing. The buck can’t stop at a thing, a software system, with nothing to lose. Q: The Bulletin piece has these interesting examples of civic feedback forums where it looks like there are real people saying things, and instead you have a barrage of comments from AI. How did you find some of these other examples in society where things go off the rails in this way?  A: After the release of ChatGPT, I started hearing a concern from people inside government who review public comments on proposed rules: a suspicion that not all of the comments were written by humans. My reaction was: That’s going to delegitimize this channel for public feedback. That was several years ago, but everyone now knows this is happening. Public comment is a pillar of democracy. You don’t just put a new rule in place. People need to have a voice and feel like they’ve been heard before a rule is imposed on them. If you skip that step, people don’t accept rules as legitimate. That’s why that process is baked into how America works. And that pillar just cracked, and by now, in my mind, it’s fallen over. Has anyone noticed? My sense is the people on the receiving end of these comments have quietly adjusted the weight they give to public comments. It was never perfect, but boy, now much of its value is being swept away.  I open my essay with this example: In 2017, the Federal Communications Commission received more than 22 million public comments on its proposal to repeal net neutrality rules, and the New York attorney general later found that nearly 18 million of them were fake. As I write in the essay, “That fraud was caught because it left fingerprints: templated text, duplicated phrasing.” But large language models erase the fingerprints. Now every comment can be fluent and different, and reviewers can no longer tell which ones express views that real people formed and stand behind. If you have enough of the stuff that’s fake — words that no one with a stake actually stands behind — it desensitizes you to what’s real. That filters back to the public, and people realize: If I take the time to express myself, they’re not even listening any more. Q: Could you say a little bit more about your point that we need people with “standing,” who will take “accountability” for all pieces of text, even when those bits of text are generated by AI?  A: In the legal system, standing is a formal idea: sometimes a case isn’t heard because the people bringing it don’t have standing. But informally we use that term all the time. I’m not trying to formalize standing in everyday life. Instead I’m asking:  What is the informal sense of the term, borrowed from the legal one, that we need to pay more attention to now? Here in New England, consider the open town meeting: The person who stands up to speak is generally expected to have standing, as someone from that town with a stake in what gets decided. And if it’s a stranger who drove from across the state, or from out of state, everyone’s like: Wait a minute, who is that? They’re not from around here. In general, there’s just enough friction and it’s costly enough to show up somewhere you don’t actually have standing, that it doesn’t happen much. Now LLMs and the current digital networked environment collapse those boundaries. We always took for granted that if someone has a voice, it’s because they have standing. They have some basis to be heard. We need to pay attention to this, and really consider how to design systems so that the people with standing are the ones who get heard.  The other idea I tried to develop is “answerability.” It isn’t formalized in law, but it’s baked into the legal process. If you have standing to give testimony, there you are, ready for cross-examination. You have to be able to answer for what you’re saying. And if you’re making a specific accusation about someone, you have to be willing to back it with facts. Standing and answerability have to travel together: The right to be heard comes with the obligation to answer for what you say. That doesn’t mean everyone has to attach their name to everything. I write in the Bulletin essay, “Privacy and answerability aren’t opposites. … An institution can verify a person and stand behind their words without exposing them.” To voice a view, you only need to show that a distinct, eligible person is speaking. An accusation asks more: Someone trusted, like a reporter, has to be able to know who is speaking. As I say: “Disclosure obligations should scale with power, and identity protections with vulnerability.” None of this means AI can’t help. AI can do a lot of the work inside the chain of accountability — drafting, summarizing, finding patterns. If someone with a stake in a rule uses AI to draft a comment, adopts it as their own, and is ready to answer for it, that’s legitimate, in this context. What AI can’t do is anchor the chain. There has to be a person at the end who stands behind the words. In the essay I lay out four design principles for building that in: “attributable authorship,” a “decomposed and inspectable process,” the use of “provenance as infrastructure,” and the need to “widen standing rather than concentrating it.” As I write, the “animating rule is that autonomy is permitted while unaccountability is not.” And the metric that matters most isn’t the efficiency gained by removing humans, but the number of people AI places into roles where they can answer for what they do. Q: There is a phrase in the documents of the Center for Constructive Communication, that we need things to move “at the speed of trust,” not at the “speed of tech.” And that implies really thinking about building up these systems. Could you just say a little more about what that phrase means to you? A: I learned that phrase when I was in Appleton, Wisconsin, with Katherine Cramer [of the University of Wisconsin], a longtime collaborator, talking with community organizers who were running “Dialogue across Divides” conversations there. They had hundreds of people involved. I thought I was developing technology tools with exactly that same purpose, and was so excited to see it. And I asked one of the people who ran that organization, “How fast did you scale this?” And he paused, and then he said, “At the speed of trust.”  And I took that to mean “slow.” Then I realized he was saying: For you, slow, because you haven’t yet earned our trust. And I’ve since learned that when you do have trust, things can move fast. So bringing in technology is really a process of engagement. It doesn’t work to say, “Trust us, we’re doing this because we think it’s for your own good.” People will turn to someone they already trust and ask, “Is this good for us?” And if that person says “Yes,” things can move fast. Look at what’s happening at the intersection of AI and society: The speed of AI and the speed of democracy are running on different clocks. Talk to people who work in democratic practice and they say, “AI must slow down, because democracy can’t move that fast.” Talk to people in AI and they say, “AI cannot slow down, democracy needs to speed up.” If we can’t get these two time scales in sync, we’re headed for a breakway situation, where AI gets deployed faster than democratic processes can respond, and decisions get made without the public. That’s starting to happen right now.  Q: We need people actively doing things to build dialogue and figure out how tech tools can interact with that. At the Center for Constructive Communication, you’ve done a few iterations of the center’s Real Talk initiatives to build civic dialogues, as well as the Youth Voices Initiative in school settings, and currently you’re working on the New Social Forms project. Could you say a few words about them?  A: The Real Talk effort represents the longest-standing thread in this work. A huge emphasis of our work has been developing better ways to listen to one another. We create a context that is always small — small is beautiful here — where people are willing to share authentically. And we have the consent architecture and the technology to reveal the larger patterns, and then share them. We’ve done this with hundreds of communities around the country. And closer to home, we’ve brought the same approach to our campus here at MIT through the realtalk@MIT program, with support from the Office of the President and the Office of the Provost, to help our community build a culture around dialogue and listening.  The second thing I’d emphasize is that we’ve been doing more and more work on deliberative processes and citizen assemblies, and on how to make them more accessible. What if a group of high schoolers says, “We have a real problem with our cellphone policy?” Suppose you want to have an assembly that brings students, teachers, and administrators together, not just to listen to people’s concerns but to make policy recommendations. So we did that. The center worked with a high school in New York City, where technology helped people reveal their preferences and differences and listen to each other. We’re also building answerability into the technology. A prototype called VoiceTrace, developed by PhD student Cassandra Overney in our group, links every output statement — a summary of what was heard in a listening process, or a recommendation coming out of a deliberation — to the specific voices behind it, so any claim can be traced back to the conversations it came from. The New Social Forms project pertains to a very interesting pattern emerging in workplaces around the world, certainly the ones we’re connected to. AI is an extraordinary tool for individual empowerment, but in the words of one of our collaborators at the Google Experience Institute, people are tunneling. They go deep, using AI to develop refined ideas, but when they surface, their ideas have diverged from their teammates’. So groups and teams trying to work together with AI, there’s a human coordination problem. We’re going to expand the initial work we’ve started with Google because there’s a lot of interest in collective communication, trust, and interaction among people trying to work together.  So is that a civic context? It’s a workplace, but workplaces are civic spaces, too. They govern people’s daily lives, they’re where many of us build civic skills and learn to cooperate across difference, and there’s a long tradition of civic life rooted in shared work. We’re all humans trying to interact with each other. These are the same issues. Justice Louis Brandeis once used the phrase “industrial democracy” to capture this. When workplaces lacked certain kinds of civic processes and civility — two interestingly related terms — labor disputes used to turn violent. Procedural justice, mediators, and people hearing one another are just as necessary in the workplace. In the end, it’s all about human beings. Hearing the humanity in one another is what democracy depends on, and it’s just as necessary for communities and organizations to function.
352ced96796d8926: From Azam Mohd
The 2027 budget raises a question Malaysians rarely ask: who bears responsibility when national promises reach citizens unevenly? The answer cannot rest with Putrajaya alone.

A budget becomes meaningful through state governments, local councils, schools, clinics and businesses. Malaysians should therefore judge this spending plan by whether public institutions can work together across administrative boundaries.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim tabled a RM460 billion federal budget on Oct 9. The finance ministry projects growth of 4.2% to 5.2% next year, while the fiscal deficit is expected to narrow to 3.3% of gross domestic product.
These forecasts are not guarantees. Their significance depends on what happens after Parliament approves expenditure and ministries begin implementation.
Consider the distance between a federal announcement and a household’s experience.

A parent may welcome education funding but still be confronted with an overcrowded classroom. A patient may hear about health allocations yet encounter long waiting times. A trader may qualify for financing but struggle with permits, infrastructure or inconsistent local enforcement.
Getting things done
None of these difficulties can be resolved by increasing appropriations alone. The missing ingredient is coordination.

Federal ministries design programmes, states control land decisions, and local authorities shape everyday business conditions. When their priorities diverge, public money can purchase activity without producing improvement.

The resulting frustration is often blamed entirely on whichever party governs nationally, although responsibility may be distributed across several institutions. This is particularly important for Sabah and Sarawak, where distance, infrastructure gaps and administrative arrangements complicate delivery. The same principle applies to rural districts in Peninsular Malaysia and densely populated urban neighbourhoods.

Equal allocations do not necessarily create equal access. A credible federal budget must recognise different costs and starting conditions without turning regional needs into partisan bargaining chips.

The 2027 budget also arrives amid uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict. Bank Negara Malaysia has announced additional financing support for smaller enterprises facing temporary cash flow pressures. Such measures can help firms survive disruption, but credit cannot repair a blocked supply route or eliminate higher transport costs. Businesses need agencies responsible for financing, logistics and trade facilitation to respond coherently together.
Delivering on promises

Malaysia, therefore, needs a delivery compact between federal and state institutions. For major programmes, the responsible ministry should identify the implementing agencies, milestones and obstacles. State governments should disclose the approvals and infrastructure commitments under their control. Local authorities should report service bottlenecks.
These arrangements would make responsibility visible without assigning every problem one political owner.

Parliament has an important role. Budget debates too often concentrate on announcements and partisan comparisons. Parliamentary committees should instead examine why comparable districts achieve different results with similar resources. Auditors can test whether procurement and implementation follow established rules, while elected representatives can question delays without alleging misconduct.
Poor performance warrants investigation; it is not, by itself, proof of corruption.

There are legitimate objections. Reporting can become bureaucratic, and states may resist federal conditions that intrude upon their constitutional responsibilities. The solution is not another elaborate national dashboard. It is a limited set of jointly agreed service standards, published responsibilities and independent verification, designed around programmes where fragmented authority obstructs delivery.
Out of the political fray

Political competition makes this more urgent. With the next general election approaching, governing parties will claim achievements while opponents highlight shortcomings. Both have legitimate democratic roles.

But citizens should be able to distinguish a policy that failed because of flawed design from one delayed by procurement, staffing, local approvals or unexpected external shocks. That distinction improves accountability rather than shielding ministers from criticism.

A useful starting point would be to select several high impact programmes spanning education, healthcare, small business support and regional connectivity. Publish who is responsible for each stage, invite state participation and review outcomes after implementation begins.
Where cooperation fails, disclose the disagreement and its consequences. Where it succeeds, retain the practice regardless of which coalition controls the relevant government.
The 2027 budget will ultimately reveal whether Malaysia can move beyond a culture in which announcing expenditure is treated as governing.

The country does not lack ambitious public promises. It needs institutions capable of delivering them together, especially when political loyalties differ. Fiscal credibility begins with sound numbers, but public confidence grows when responsibility is shared, visible and impossible to evade.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
23be0a5665a7f0e9: Dunia ini umpama sebuah penjara yang besar dan dipenuhi dengan segala macam hantu. Itu agaknya yang cuba disampaikan oleh Joko Anwar melalui filem arahannya, Ghost in the Cell. Saya tidak tahu apa genre paling tepat untuk filem ini. Komedi seram absurd barangkali tetapi dalam komedi ada serius dan misteri, ada keganasan, ada aksi ala kartun. Semuanya bercampur, mencetuskan kecelaruan. Joko mungkin mahu menyatakan yang hidup ini beginilah, penuh dengan kecelaruan ragam dan identiti. Malah ada babak yang mengarut sehingga saya teringat filem Kung Fu Hustle arahan Stephen Chow.

Filem Ghost in the Cell ini turut menampilkan dua nama dari Malaysia, Bront Palarae yang memegang watak Jefry, seorang pegawai penjara dan Ho Yuhang sebagai Rendra, seorang banduan yang merupakan ketua sindiket dadah. Ho yang lebih dikenali sebagai pengarah filem membawakan watak penjenayah bertubuh kecil tetapi cukup digeruni.

Cerita bermula dengan Dimas (Endy Arfian), seorang wartawan yang dituduh membunuh ketuanya lalu dihumban ke penjara Labuhan Angsana. Di situ dia bertemu pelbagai jenis manusia, termasuk Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya), seorang banduan yang sering membela orang lain walaupun tindakannya menyebabkan hukuman penjaranya bertambah. Watak Anggoro memperlihatkan satu paradoks. Dia memang pesalah di sisi undang-undang tetapi masih mempunyai rasa kemanusiaan yang tinggi. Sebaliknya, ketua penjara yang diberikan kuasa menjaga undang-undang pula bersifat binatang atau hantu dalam mengejar pangkat dan kedudukan.

Di penjara itu juga ada Tokek (Aming), banduan ganas yang menjadikan keganasan seksual sebagai alat menakutkan orang lain. Dimas yang baru masuk penjara menjadi sasarannya. Tokek mewakili manusia buas dan gemar membuli orang yang lebih lemah. Melihatkan wajahnya sahaja sudah cukup membuat kita menggeletar. Bagaimanapun, dia mati akhirnya setelah gagal mempertahankan diri apabila berhadapan dengan hantu yang ternyata lebih perkasa. Tokek adalah gambaran manusia yang sebenarnya tidaklah kuat mana tetapi hanya berani kerana dia tahu pihak yang dibuli itu sudah sememangnya penakut. Dia memanipulasi keadaan.

Apa yang menarik perhatian saya ialah cara hantu dalam filem ini membunuh mangsanya. Mayat mangsa disusun dan digubah seakan sebuah arca seni. Ini bagai satu metafora yang menarik. Ia tentang kita yang kadangkala menggambarkan keindahan dengan mempergunakan penderitaan orang lain. Arca memanglah cantik dan hebat tetapi ia dibuat menggunakan mayat yang penuh darah dengan isi perut yang terburai, biji mata terkeluar dan sendi yang patah. Manusia begitulah, mempergunakan hidup pihak lain demi mencari keuntungan dengan menjual gossip dan fitnah, hiburan atau berita buruk tentang mereka. Dan kita gembira menikmati keindahannya sebagai bahan tontonan tanpa mempedulikan kesengsaraan di sebaliknya.

Lebih menarik lagi dalam Ghost in the Cell ini ialah hantu yang membunuh itu akan menyerupai mangsanya sendiri ketika menyerang. Ia seolah-olah manusia itu akhirnya dibunuh oleh kejahatan yang terpelihara di dalam tubuhnya sendiri. Hantu bukan datang dari luar, tetapi dari dalam kita sendiri.

Satu lagi watak yang menarik ialah Six (Yoga Pratama), banduan yang tidak berpegang kepada agama tetapi mempunyai kebolehan melihat hantu dan aura manusia. Ini satu lagi paradoks. Selalunya orang alim yang lebih memahami perkara ghaib. Tetapi dalam filem ini, orang yang tidak beragama pula mampu melihat sesuatu yang gagal dilihat oleh orang lain. Saya melihatnya sebagai sindiran, kerana manusia tak kira apa bangsa atau agama pun tetap dikurniakan tuhan dengan kelebihan masing-masing tetapi adakalanya kelebihan yang diberikan itu tidak mampu difahami olehnya sendiri dan dia perlukan bimbingan. Maka itu, banduan alim bernama Wildan (Mike Lucock) diperlukan untuk mentafsir warna-warna aura yang dilihat oleh Six. Wildan tak mampu melihat aura yang keluar dari tubuh manusia seperti mana Six, tetapi dia mempunyai keilmuan untuk mentafsirkannya. Nah! Begitulah tahap manusia dalam memahami, mempercayai dan menghayati sesuatu. Faham, percaya dan menghayati adalah tiga perkara yang cukup besar bezanya.

Di dalam filem ini, tertarik kepada manusia yang mempunyai aura negatif seperti kemarahan dan kebencian. Untuk mengelakkan diri daripada menjadi mangsa, banduan perlu menenangkan fikiran dan mengawal emosi. Ada yang memilih untuk bersembahyang, ada pula yang menari. Sembahyang merupakan ritual yang menghubungkan manusia dengan tuhan, sedangkan menari lazimnya dianggap kegiatan hiburan. Tetapi dalam filem ini, kedua-duanya boleh menghasilkan ketenangan yang diperlukan untuk menghindari hantu. Yang hendak diperlihatkan bukanlah soal cara mana lebih suci atau lebih baik, tetapi bagaimana manusia mencari ketenangan melalui jalan yang berbeza. Maknanya, ketenangan hati itu penting biarpun kita berbeza pegangan. Tetapi di dalam dunia yang bernama penjara, mereka terpaksa mencari apa saja persamaan untuk terus hidup dengan selamat. Untuk selamat, manusia perlu tenang.

Kemudian kita diperkenalkan kepada Prakasa Kitabuming (Arswendy Bening Swara), seorang politikus dan ahli perniagaan berpengaruh yang menjalani hukuman penjara tetapi masih menikmati kemewahan. Dalam penjara yang sama, ada orang yang hidup berhimpit dan terdedah kepada keganasan, sedangkan orang tertentu masih boleh menikmati layanan istimewa. Sepatutnya apabila seseorang dihukum, pangkat dan kedudukannya tidak lagi memberikan keistimewaan. Orang biasa masuk penjara kehilangan kebebasan. Orang berpengaruh masuk penjara masih boleh bermewah-mewahan. Ada pula watak Sapto sebagai Ketua Penjara yang mempunyai cita-cita besar menjadi Menteri sehingga sanggup tersengih-sengih dan melutut demi membodek Prakasa, politikus yang menjadi penghuni penjaranya sendiri.

Sebenarnya hantu itu mahu mencari Prakasa. Hantu mengikut Dimas ketika Dimas meninjau kawasan hutan Kalimantan yang musnah angkara Prakasa. Tetapi, dalam usaha memburu Prakasa ramai yang menjadi korban. Prakasa menemui ajalnya dengan cukup sinis. Dia berhadapan dengan hantu yang menyerupai dirinya ketika muda, ketika dia konon masih seorang pejuang yang mempunyai cita-cita dan prinsip. Dia adalah gambaran pejuang muda yang telah mengkhianati prinsip perjuangannya setelah berada di puncak kuasa. Hantu yang membunuhnya adalah diri mudanya sendiri yang pernah berapi-api berjuang. Rupanya si pejuang ini telah menjadi tawanan kepada pangkat dan kuasa.

Ada satu babak, kita diperlihatkan dengan sekumpulan banduan artis dan selebriti yang diasingkan daripada kumpulan Dimas dan Anggoro. Dialog lucunya ialah ‘rakyat Indonesia lebih mengambil berat nasib artis daripada nasibnya sendiri'. Saya ketawa kerana sindiran itu bukan masalah di Indonesia sahaja. Kita di sini pun sama. Kita boleh bergaduh siapa betul siapa salah bila artis bercerai dan berantak, kita sanggup masukkan duit di dalam akaun bank pempengaruh media sosial yang mengadu perniagaannya bakal melingkup kerana hutang yang membebankan sedangkan apabila sepupu kita hendak menjual dodol buatannya sendiri, kita tak jawab WhatsApp dia langsung. Kita simpati kepada artis yang sedang sakit tetapi jiran sebelah sudah sebulan terlantar di wad, kita tak jenguk pun. Memang kita semua obses dengan artis dan selebriti.

Joko melihat penjara bukan sekadar set penggambaran dan premis penceritaan. Ia adalah dunia. Dunia boleh jadi syurga jika semua manusianya tenang dan damai tetapi dunia boleh jadi sebuah kurungan yang menakutkan jika di dalamnya bercampur antara manusia baik dengan manusia durjana. Di dalam filem ini digambarkan manusia ada yang mahu berkuasa, ada yang mahu dilindungi, ada yang mahu dipuja dan ada yang sekadar mahu terus hidup. Hantu adalah dosa silam yang memburu manusia itu sendiri untuk menghukum jika manusia tersebut masih tidak mahu berubah menjadi insan yang baik. Di tengah-tengah seram, ngeri, takut dan cemas itu kita masih ada ruang untuk ketawa. Sepertinya kita faham bahawa dunia ini hanyalah senda-gurau sementara sahaja.

Memang semenjak dua ini saya sering menulis tentang filem dan teater yang saya tonton. Ini kerana apa yang ingin saya sampaikan dalam tulisan berkenaan kehidupan telah berjaya dipersembahkan oleh mereka dalam bentuk visual. Saya tidak pastilah tafsiran saya menepati apa yang dimaksudkan oleh karyawan asalnya tetapi inilah yang boleh saya kutip untuk dikongsi bersama. Untuk kita renungi kehidupan ini melalui sebuah persembahan kreatif.

Sebuah karya yang sudah dipertontonkan kepada masyarakat tidak semestinya mempunyai satu tafsiran yang wajib dipatuhi. Kita bebas menterjemahnya. Apa yang saya lihat dalam filem ini adalah tentang perangai manusia yang terpenjara akibat menjadi mangsa kepada nafsu buas sendiri. Nafsu manusia memang tak pernah puas. Jika ada peluang untuk naik, manusia akan naik walaupun akan menindas manusia lain. Dari situlah wujudnya dendam dan pembalasan oleh pihak yang teraniaya. Hantu dalam Ghost in the Cell itu muncul pun kerana manusialah yang mengundangnya. Telah kita pelajari di dalam kitab al-Quran, manusia adalah sebaik-baik kejadian dan makhluk terbaik ini jugalah yang sedang menghancur-musnahkan dunia.

d4e994a42990ef49: From Moaz Nair

The ghost of Malay politics past continues to haunt a fading Umno. Ever since its historic, humiliating downfall in the 2018 general election, the party has been trapped in a state of pathetic paralysis, desperately daydreaming about reclaiming its crown as the nation's undisputed political hegemon.

Yet, instead of executing a clear strategy, Umno's leadership is caught in a dilemma of cowardly choices: suck up to Pakatan Harapan in a volatile unity government, or venture into the wilderness alone, or crawl back to its treacherous former rival PAS.

This delusional "two-tier approach" – trying to play both sides by cutting different deals at the state and federal levels – is a weak political gimmick that has failed to fool anyone, least of all PAS.

Meanwhile, Umno’s relationship with PH has rapidly soured under its current leadership. By even flirting with PAS, a party that relentlessly trashes PH as secular and liberal, Umno is actively incinerating whatever fragile trust it has left with its current governing partners.
Let’s call a spade a spade: this is a desperate, toxic battle for survival.

After bloating itself on power for nearly six decades, Umno still blindly demands to be treated as the "Big Brother" of Malay politics. But wake up: PAS now holds the actual cards. Armed with a superior parliamentary seat count and total control over four state governments -- Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis -- PAS has effectively usurped the throne.
Walking into a trap

Analysts see right through Umno’s terror. The party knows that any formal alliance with the Islamic juggernaut will reduce Umno to the position of a weak, castrated junior partner. History has proven time and again that when these two egos clash over who commands Malay politics, a bloody political knife-fight is virtually guaranteed.
Besides, how short is Umno's memory?

The catastrophic collapse of the 2019 Muafakat Nasional pact should have been a permanent lesson. PAS didn't hesitate to stab Umno in the back, secretly conspiring with Bersatu to form Perikatan Nasional in 2020. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi openly branded that move a betrayal, and the party rank and file still rightly whisper that PAS carries a "DNA of betrayal".
To walk back into that trap is pure political suicide.

Any attempt at a reunion faces brutal realities: PAS will never surrender the safe, Malay-majority seats it currently locks down. It will greedily force Umno to run in highly volatile, hostile areas, guaranteeing an electoral wipeout of Umno's remaining footprint.

PAS’s aggressive youth wing and top leaders are no longer hiding their ambitions: they want a PAS prime minister. They will never yield the top job to a diminished Umno, shattering any illusion of an equal partnership.
Can Umno survive?

Umno’s traditional lifeline has always been its ability to bridge gaps using non-Malay votes. Crawling into bed with an uncompromising Islamist party will permanently alienate those voters, severing Umno's last remaining oxygen supply.

This desperate anxiety is already reeking at the state level. In Perak and Pahang, Umno leaders hold the posts of menteri besar only out of sheer charity by PH, not because Umno commands a real majority. Inviting PAS into these states is code for a hostile takeover. PAS will effortlessly leverage its momentum, hijack the state machinery, and relegate Umno to political irrelevance on its own turf.

PAS knows it doesn't need Umno; its most realistic path to absolute power remains firmly rooted in consolidating its Malay-Islamic framework. This leaves Umno stranded at a historic crossroads of its own making. Going solo in today’s fractured landscape offers zero guarantee of survival, yet leaping back into the arms of PAS ensures complete subordination to a green wave that has already captured the Malay-Muslim electorate.

If Umno wants to survive, it needs to snap out of its historical delusion. It can no longer demand the "Big Brother" crown based on past glory. It must adapt to a brutal new reality or get comfortable being buried in the footnotes of Malaysian history.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

d4cc7aabe8176b8f: For decades, South Asia was locked in a perpetual cycle of conflict management: brief military clashes between India and Pakistan would be followed by de-escalation and the resumption of formal peace talks, which eventually gave way to another bout of conflict. But this pattern has now been broken.

No high-level dialogue has taken place since 2016. Rather than some temporary diplomatic tantrum, this reflects a paradigm shift in Indian foreign policy, permanently altering the subcontinent’s security architecture.

The roots of this stalemate can be found in the structural failures of past diplomacy. In 1947, 1965, and 1971, Pakistan initiated conventional wars, none of which delivered the results it desired. The third resulted in the breakup of the country and the birth of independent Bangladesh.

These experiences, together with the success of the US-backed mujahideen in their fight against Soviet forces in Afghanistan in the late 1980s, prompted Pakistan’s military to embrace a new strategy, based on asymmetrical warfare—or, more bluntly, terrorism.
From 1989 to 1993, as terrorist attacks caused significant civilian casualties in India, Pakistani officers crowed about “bleeding India to death by a thousand cuts”.
Indian leaders were nonetheless convinced that structured dialogue could persuade Pakistan to abandon this strategy. This belief gave rise to the Composite Dialogue framework in the late 1990s.
This bureaucratic mechanism was designed to segment contentious issues—ranging from Kashmir to trade and humanitarian concerns—so that friction in one area would not derail progress in others.
There was just one problem: every major Indian peace overture was met with an act of military or terrorist provocation that the Pakistani government was either unable or unwilling to prevent.

In 1999, when then-Indian prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee undertook his historic bus journey to Lahore to sign a landmark peace declaration, Pakistani troops were infiltrating the Kargil district of Ladakh—actions that led to the Kargil War (which Pakistan lost).

In 2008, when back-channel diplomacy was on the brink of delivering a non-territorial solution to the Kashmir issue, coordinated terrorist attacks by Pakistan-based militants killed 166 innocent civilians in Mumbai.

This cycle exposed a profound institutional disconnect within Pakistan. Its civilian governments lacked the authority or longevity to fulfill the commitments they made at the negotiating table, and its military-intelligence apparatus viewed peace with India as an existential threat to its domestic hegemony.

Now, India has had enough. Prime Minister Narendra Modi initially followed the old peacemaking script. He invited his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, to his 2014 inauguration, and visited Lahore the following year.
Even when this visit was followed by a terrorist attack on the Indian airbase in Pathankot, Modi invited Sharif to join the official investigation into the incident.
Then came the final straw: Pakistan’s joint investigation team concluded that the attack was a “drama staged by India to malign Pakistan”.

With that, India abandoned its doctrine of strategic restraint in favour of a new guiding dictum: talks and terror cannot coexist. India would return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantled, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

This diplomatic shift was accompanied by a fundamental change in India’s military doctrine. For nearly three decades, Pakistan assumed that its tactical nuclear arsenal would deter India from launching conventional military reprisals for terrorist attacks. Then India decided to call Pakistan’s bluff—most notably, in last year’s “Operation Sindoor”.

Through calibrated retaliatory actions, ranging from surgical cross-border strikes to sophisticated aerial bombardments targeting terrorist infrastructure deep within Pakistani territory, India demonstrated a willingness to accept escalation risks to impose tangible costs on its neighbour.
By signalling that state-sponsored terror would automatically trigger a conventional military response, India has sought to rewrite the rules of deterrence in South Asia.
The current stalemate is hardly desirable. The absence of a diplomatic safety valve between nuclear-armed neighbours poses acute risks to regional, even global, stability.

Even the most basic bilateral matters, such as humanitarian issues, trade blockades, and water sharing, are now viewed through a hyper-politicised national-security lens. And if a new crisis erupts, what mechanism is available to manage it? The margin for miscalculation is perilously thin.

But the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak. Pakistan’s military leadership still pins its domestic political legitimacy partly on hostility towards India, even as the country faces profound economic distress. And India, with its growing economic and conventional-military advantages, has little reason to compromise on its core security interests.

The US is certainly not encouraging India to rethink this stance. Not only has Donald Trump’s administration all but abandoned America’s Indo-Pacific strategy, in which India played a central role as a critical counterweight to a rising China, it has also embraced Pakistan, which, despite its financial instability and close ties with China, has managed to woo the US administration by striking a lucrative cryptocurrency deal with a Trump-linked firm and unctuously nominating Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize.

With the underpinnings of the India-Pakistan conflict firmly entrenched, the current stalemate should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate strategy of disengagement.

Until Pakistan undergoes a political transformation that fundamentally alters its security calculus, or a “black swan” event forces an existential realignment of regional priorities, the silence across the subcontinent will endure—and the risk of catastrophic error will remain.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and human resource development, is a fourth-term elected MP for the opposition Indian National Congress.

6e25bbbe74d1c5c9: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights. This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
